maintopic: CHARGES BY HON. G. N. GORDON MOTION FOR PRINTING OF PROCEEDINGS AND EVIDENCE

speechtext:
Mr. G. R. GEARY (South Toronto) presented the first report of the special committee appointed to inquire into certain charges made by the Hon. G. N. Gordon,
K.C., as follows:
Your committee recommend that 500 copies in English and 250 copies in French of proceedings and evidence which may be taken be printed, as required, and that standing order 64 be suspended in relation thereto.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
Mr. GEARY moved that the report be concurred in.
Right Hon. \V. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):	May I say with
respect to this motion for the printing in English and French of five hundred copies of the proceedings of the committee which is investigating certain allegations made by the Hon. Mr. Gordon, that I think it is a waste of public money to print the proceedings of this committee. What useful purpose is going to be served by it? The Prime Minister wishes to have certain facts brought out and no doubt a statement by Mr. Gordon in reference thereto. This will be brought out in committee and the committee can make its report, but surely it is simply throwing away the
Privilege-Mr. Gott

money of the people, which it is difficult enough to raise through taxation these days, to spend it on the recording and printing of the evidence of a committee functioning for the purpose for which this committee is functioning. I submit again that this matter should never have been brought into parliament at all, and I believe the less there is of record concerning it the better it will be for the Prime Minister and all concerned. I protest against the printing.
Motion agreed to, on division.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR CONSIDERATION ON AGENDA OF IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, February 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. MacLean and the amendment thereto of Mr. Irvine.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR CONSIDERATION ON AGENDA OF IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE
speechtext:
The resolution placed before this house by the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, if the empire is to become an economic unit, the stabilization of currency within the empire is very important and should be one of the first questions for consideration on the agenda of the Imperial conference at its meeting in July next.
Stabilization oj Currency

Later in the debate the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) moved the following amendment:
That the motion be amended by striking out all the words after the word "that" in the first line and substituting therefor the following:
in the opinion of this house the Canadian representatives at the coming Imperial economic conference should move for the stabilization of the currency of all British countries to be on a basis other than gold.
Continuing this debate, Mr. Speaker, I wish first of all to congratulate the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) upon bringing before this house one of the most important subjects it has been our lot to consider. The matter of currency and credit is very closely linked with the trade, commerce, welfare and the happiness of the people of any country. I am only sorry that we have not heard a single word in support of the resolution he proposed to the house from any other member of the group to which he belongs.
I wish however to congratulate the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) who in his speech in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne criticized the government by stating that in the speech from the throne no mention had been made of the subject of currency and credit. He drew attention to the importance of this subject and wondered whether in view of the crisis we are going through the government of the day was quite satisfied with the present situation and whether our present condition could not in some degree be traced to the unsound state of currency and credit. In making that reference however the right hon. gentleman travelled a long way from the stand he took only a year ago when I had the privilege of moving a subamendment on behalf of the group to which I have the honour to belong, to the off ecu that we should go off the gold basis, so far as holding gold behind our currency was concerned. At that particular time the right hon. gentleman criticized me severely for making such a suggestion. Since that time however much water has passed under the bridge; Great Britain and many other countries have gone off the gold basis and, the subject being now more popular, it is of course in order for anyone who wishes to climb upon the proverbial band wagon.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) decided to take part in this debate, naturally we anticipated something of a constructive nature from him, particularly because of his great ability and because of the important portfolio for which he is responsible. I was therefore very much surprised when, in the
rMr. Spencer.]
short time he spoke, he treated the subject rather lightly and did his best to criticize the efforts of the hon. member who brought the resolution before the house. Continuing the debate, an amendment was moved by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) upon which I should like to congratulate him, and which, if accepted will, in my view, add weight to the motion. I should like also to congratulate the hon. member upon the very able manner in which he presented his argument to the house. We know that for many years he has given this subject a great deal of thought and from time to time has placed his views before this house. I do not think however that he has ever made a more able speech and one more to the point than he made the other day.
I should like to remind the house of a statement by C. E. Neill, who before his death was vice-president of the Royal Bank, to which reference was made by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) and which reads as follows:
If the central banks of all the countries on a gold basis should deliberately adopt a common policy they could within a certain time lag. raise or lower the price level almost at will.
I entirely agree with that statement. Unfortunately, however, countries do not pull together in this regard and prices are not regulated because we have not international cooperative effort. In this connection may I refer to a very able address given by Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, president of the Midland Bank of Great Britain who, speaking to the shareholders of that bank is reported in the Manchester Guardian of January 30. as follows:
We must have a managed gold standard by an international agreement or we must definitely abandon gold and rely on a managed standard of credit and currency without any metallic basis at all.
Further, he stated:
The time has gone by for the child-like belief that as long as a country is on a gold standard all is well.
And, further:
The world crisis is due in part to the inefficient "working of our monetary machinery.
Making a study of this subject I come to the conclusion that we face an inevitable collapse of our financial structure so long as we try to tie ourselves to a gold basis. I remember that in the year 1923, when the Bank Act was under revision, and before that time when an investigation was being made into the basis of credit, its function, control, and relation to trade, one

Stabilization of Currency
of the witnesses placed before the committee a graph in the shape of an inverted pyramid showing the position of the Canadian monetary system, and indicating very cleverly the way that the monetary system was, supposedly, built on a small basis of gold. It showed, as it would show to-day if a similar figure were drawn, that we have only a small basis of gold in Canada, and that on top of that there is an amount of currency nearly three times the amount of gold, and payable in gold

and I say "and payable in gold" because although private bank currency is not payable in gold it is payable in dominion notes, which are payable in gold. Therefore we might make the blanket statement that all the notes used are payable in gold. On top of that we have bank deposits aggregating to-day about two billion dollars. Then, above that, we have bonds which, in round figures, aggregate approximately $2,300,000,000, all of which are supposed to be payable in gold. It is manifest that all those notes and securities could not possibly be redeemed in gold. Indeed, if we required redemption in gold, that is, if we applied the gold basis strictly, there would not be a solvent bank in this country. Of course, the gold basis is perfectly all right when it is not called upon to function; in other words, it is a matter of imagination, and the sooner we realize that the better for all concerned. That this is so, I need only remind the house that whenever there is a world crisis, whenever we are in a state of war, whenever trade is particularly bad-as it is to-day-then we promptly go off the gold basis; the government passes an order in council or secures legislation declaring that paper currency may be redeemed in other than gold.
It is interesting to realize that our monetary system is made up largely of three things: coin, currency, and credit. Coin tG-day, we use to the extent of about $31,000,000; currency varies anywhere from $300,000,000 to $400,000,000; as to the balance, according to the statement made by Sir Edmund Walker in 1923, no less than 96 per cent of our monetary transactions are carried on by the checking system. The amount of money therefore can be increased or decreased entirely at the wish of those who have the control of credit. At this point I should like to bring to my aid a statement by the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, He asks the question:
How can the supply of money be increased?
This is his answer;
The amount of money in existence varies only with the action of the banks in increasing or
diminishing deposits. We know how this is effected. Every bank loan creates a deposit, and every repayment of a bank loan destroys one.
I know some hon. gentlemen will contend that that is a reversal of the process that takes place; some of them still think that our loans are all created from savings deposits.
I should like to remind them, however, that if that were the fact the more loans you made from pre-existing deposits, the smaller amount of savings deposits you would have. But instead of that, a study of the bank returns will show that the more loans made the greater the amount of the deposits; the more loans cancelled, the smaller the amount of deposits will be. In his book on the Elements of Banking, Mr. H. D. Macleod writes:
The essential and distinctive feature of a "bank" and a "banker" is to issue credit payable on demand, and this credit may be put into circulation .... and serve as money.
The manner of creating money was brought to our attention most pointedly during the late war. At that time we needed a great deal more goods to carry on our part in the great conflict. This involved a larger supply of money, and this supply was secured through the issue of bonds. This action would have had no effect at all on prices so long as on the one hand we put more money into circulation and on the other hand we created an extra quantity of goods; or if after creating these goods we had destroyed them, and had also cancelled the additional amount of money put into circulation; in either case prices would have remained stationary. But instead of that, while we destroyed a great quantity of goods in the theatre of war, 94 per cent of the new money was left in circulation. Therefore we had a larger amount of money in circulation in proportion to the quantity of goods on hand. Naturally this had the effect of increasing prices. Again and again large sums of new money were put into circulation, and each time the same thing occurred-most of the new goods being destroyed while the greater part of the new money was kept in circulation. Consequently at the end of the war we found we had to pay very high prices for everything.
Now, it had taken a number of years to inflate the currency in that way, and the only fair thing would have been to deflate this currency-if deflation was necessary-over a number of years equal to the period during which inflation had taken place. Instead, a drastic deflation was brought about. I might say that a gradual inflation is always a good thing for the producers, for it is always to their benefit to produce for a rising market; on
Stabilization of Currency

the other hand, the investors, particularly bondholders, lose to a certain extent, because they do not get any more interest on their bonds to compensate for the higher cost of living. But deflation is always a very bad thing for producers-and they compose the major part of our population-because they do not want to produce for a falling market; by contrast, however, the investors are correspondingly benefited, because their revenue is not diminished and they have the advantage of the lowered cost of living.
Now, what happened after the war? Let me again quote Mr. McKenna. He points out that in Great Britain'-and the same thing occurred here:
A policy of deflation could only end in the strangulation of business and widespread unemployment. Such a policy had already received public official sanction. Unhappily, employment decreased month by month as this policy was enforced.
On the same point I diesire to cite Mr. J. M. Keynes as follows:
Deflation . . . involves a transference of wealth from the rest of the community to the rentier class and -to all holders of titles of money. In particular it involves a transference from all borrowers ... to lenders.
At this point I should like to pay a well-deserved compliment to Mr. Keynes on the remarkable fulfilment of the prophecy he made in 1919. It will be remembered that in an advisory capacity to the British delegates, he took an active part during the negotiations which resulted in the treaty of Versailles. Then he resigned and wrote a book entitled The Economic Consequences of the Peace, from which I take this passage:
The war has ended with everyone owing everyone else immense sums of money. Germany owes a large sum to the Allies; the Allies owe a large sum to Great Britain; and Great Britain owes a large sum to the United States.
The holders of war loan in every country are owed a large sum by the state; and the state in its turn is owed a large sum by these and other taxpayers.
The whole position is misleading, artificial, and vexatious. We shall never be able to move again unless we can free our limbs of these paper shackles. A general bonfire is such a necessity that unless we can make of it an orderly and good-tempered affair in which no serious injustice is done to anyone, it will, when it comes at last, grow into a conflagration that may destroy much else as well.
In his very interesting book entitled The Story of Canada's War Finance, Sir Thomas White gives us most interesting details of what was done during that period. I should like to give two small quotations from that book. The first is from page 17, where the author says:

In a word, we paid the cost of our military operations by our production during the war.
I often wonder how our returned soldiers felt, coming back from the war, knowing a statement such as this had been made and knowing it to be true, yet having to do their share to pay for the war all over again. Then on page 59 Sir Thomas White said:
The burden of the debt created is passed on to future generations as a legacy and reminder of the waste of war.
I take it, Mr. Speaker, that there is no need for gold at all behind internal currency, and I was very pleased to read Mr. McKenna's speech in the Manchester Guardian, to which I have already referred. He supports this and many other contentions made from this corner of the house during the last ten years. I should like to refer also to another very able man. Sir Basil Blanchet, a director of the Bank of England, who spoke to the Canadian Club of Ottawa only about a year ago. At that time he said there was absolutely no need for gold behind internal currency, that it should be limited only by legislation and that there should be no limitation until there was an ample supply to meet the requirements of the public for a medium of exchange in the transferring of goods and services from one to another. As I said before, gold never has stood up in a crisis; it never will, and the sooner we get rid of it as a pure make-believe the better for all concerned.
No doubt there is value to gold in settling international balances, but the gold we have at present cost us a lot of money, and we are making nothing out of it. We might as well take that gold and use it as it is needed to pay our debts, and in that way we would save a great deal of the interest we have to pay at present. With the amount of gold we have on hand this would make a very considerable saving in our interest charges, for I want to remind the house that last year we paid no less than $124,000,000 in interest on our national debt.
I might quote various other authorities in support of the stand I have taken; I should like to mention Major C. H. Douglas, of London, England; Professor Soddy of Oxford university, Professor Irving Fisher of Columbia university, and many others who have given this matter a great deal of thought.
To-day we are going through a period of contraction of credit. No one, no matter what may be his business, but has had a great deal of difficulty in getting credit for the last couple of years, irrespective of security. What does contraction of credit mean? First it means a crash in prices, then a collapse of

Stabilization of Cunency
trade and following that, inevitably, a great increase in unemployment. The only silver lining I can see in the cloud at present is that this crisis is man made, and therefore it can be man mended. I do not believe humanity is going to be so insane as to let this crisis reach such a pitch that chaos will rule supreme; I believe some remedy will be found which will prevent the present rapid drift towards a chaotic condition in the world. If I were to make one sugegstion- and I could make many-it would be that the government form what might be termed a finance statistical bureau, whose first duty would be to keep very close tab on price levels and to recommend to the government and to the banks, since those are the two agencies through which credit or currency is issued at the present time, when to contract or when to expand credit, because it is the total quantity of money available to be spent that determines price levels.
In the speech from the throne we were told that world conditions are beyond the control of the Canadian people. That may be so, but our share of world control is not beyond the reach of the Canadian people and, as part of the world, it is up to us through whatever government may be in power to put forward some remedy to try to rectify the situation which faces us to-day. If we cannot make an international agreement we can make the next best thing, an agreement between all the British countries, and at the Imperial conference to be held here next July Canada will have an opportunity to bring forward such a resolution as we are considering to-day, together with the amendment which has been suggested, for consideration by the best brains attending that conference, in order to seek some means whereby the present serious drift will be checked and conditions brought back to normalcy.
In studying this question I have often thought how we have become turned around in so many things. For instance, when all is said and done, money should be nothing more or less than a medium of exchange for goods or services as between man and man. Instead of that, and instead of making money a slave to humanity as it should be, humanity certainly has become a slave to money, or to finance and those who control it.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct the attention of the house to some of the practical disadvantages to Canada of the erratic system under which we allow ourselves to be controlled. For instance, we find that it is possible for Australia to dump wheat into Vancouver in competition with the farmers 41761-33
of the prairie provinces, who as we all know are producing wheat to-day at a great loss. That is an extraordinary situation, and it has been brought about largely because of the difference between the currencies of the two countries. I know of one association which sends cattle to Great Britain, and which has lost no less than $19,000 for the same reason. It is because of these reasons that I sincerely hope the house and the government will give very sympathetic consideration to the motion and amendment now before us, so that when the Imperial conference meets in Ottawa in July of this year these matters will be brought forward in the hope that something worth while may be done.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR CONSIDERATION ON AGENDA OF IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the tremendous importance of the subject which is included within the ambit of the resolution and the amendment warrants, I think, the most careful consideration of the house, and so far as I am concerned I am anxious to give to it the closest study. I think I can say on behalf of the government that it is intensely interested in and impressed with the importance of the subject. Before giving expression to the few thoughts I have on the subject generally, I should like to offer an amendment to the amendment, 'because possibly it will place this question in a somewhat better light. The resolution itself was a little innocuous and was very general. I was rather sorry that the hon. member who introduced it (Mr. MacLean) did not enlighten the house as to just what he meant, what he wished or what he hoped for, and consequently I am not able to interpret correctly what he did have in his mind. The amendment is one to which we have no great objection except in one particular, and that is that it is more or less a contradiction. It asks of the economic conference that an effort be made towards the stabilization of the currencies of the British countries, but in the last clause it puts an absolute estoppel upon the gold basis-it must be on a basis other than gold. In other words, the amendment asks the house to request the Imperial conference to study the question but it ties the hands of the conference, so far as Canada is concerned if parliament adopts this resolution as it stands, in regard to the inclusion of gold as a basis for money under any consideration. I have therefore an amendment to move to the amendment, and I offer it not in any spirit of criticism of the efforts of my hon. friends opposite but rather to

Stabilization oj Currency

bring the question into a form that would be more acceptable. I beg to move in amendment to the amendment:
That all the words after the word "conference" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"Should initiate and support measures for the stabilization of the currencies of all British countries in such manner as to facilitate trade between the component parts of the empire and to promote economic unity therein."
As thus amended, the resolution would read:
That, in the opinion of this house, the Canadian representatives at the coming Imperial economic conference should initiate and support measures for the stabilization of the currencies of all British countries in such manner as to facilitate trade between the component parts of the empire and to promote economic unity therein.
I wish to preface by one or two general observations a necessarily 'brief study of the question of currencies, money and so forth. I believe that if we are to give this matter intelligent consideration we ought to keep in mind certain major factors, certain conditions that exist, whether we like it or not, and endeavour to study the problem from an impartial standpoint and in the light of all these factors. I do not presume for a moment that in the brief time at my disposal I shall be able to present to the house all the factors, but I Shall hope to present some of the factors that enter into this very important subject.
In the first place, I would point out that our difficulties to-day are not of a domestic origin; they are largely of international origin. In saying this I am not for a moment seeking to relieve the government of the day of any responsibility; I am not seeking to evade the responsibility, shall I say, for coping with conditions within Canada. But I do wish to face the cold facts, and I say that the most serious difficulty that we have in this country in regard to commodity prices-whether it be lumber, fish, iron, lead, silver, zinc, copper and so on, any or all of these things-the difficulty arising from low commodity prices, is due to international or worldwide factors which must be faced and dealt with before we can hope for any definite change in conditions. Again, I would emphasize the fact that these conditions cannot be changed by any purely Canadian effort; it will require the effort not only of Canada and of the countries within the British Empire, but the efforts of the countries of the world before we can hope to overcome the present difficulties.
May I in passing point out certain facts. It will be recalled, for instance, that during the past few years, that is to say, prior to a year and a half ago-the period following the war 
and up to that time

Great Britain has made an heroic effort to assist in the financing of the affairs of the countries of Europe. And particularly is this so in regard to Germany. Recognizing that it was absolutely essential that Germany should be given the wherewithal to function economically before she could be expected to pay reparations, Britain rendered assistance to that country heroically, to the degree of jeopardizing her own interests. As a matter of fact, when these loans to Germany and other countries became frozen it resulted in the collapse of the gold standard in England. That was the extent to which Great Britain went. The result of all this was, as I say, that Britain went off the gold standard. Moreover, Great Britain in the meantime found her exports decreasing and her imports increasing to such an extent that it became impossible for her as a country to carry on. Another thing that happened to the mother country was this. As a direct result of her efforts to assist Germany and other countries in Europe there was a flight of capital from Great Britain. In France, for instance, they realized that the British policy was one which would endanger the financial stability of the country and they withdrew their deposits from London. The result of that was, among other things, to force Great Britain off the gold standard. Another very considerable factor in this worldwide financial collapse was the tremendous amount of loans made by the United States in South America and other parts of the world. Perhaps the South American loans were the most disastrous. Many of these loans have been virtually repudiated, involving hundreds of millions of dollars. If they have not been repudiated legally they have simply been allowed to go by the board so far as paying either interest or principal is concerned. The result has been that the United States in turn has lost tremendous sums of money abroad. Then add to that the well known and oft cited fact of the burden of debt which is resting on the necks of the people the world over, nationally, internationally and individually.
I sometimes think that the present day condition, taking the world picture of debt, is very similar to the condition which obtained, if I recall my history correctly, in the little republic when Solon took charge. I recall that one of the first acts on his part was to release the people from debt. So burdensome and terrific had become the debt of the people that many natural born citizens of that country had mortgaged their bodies, their lives, to other people as a security for debt. So

Stabilization oj Currency
burdensome had the situation become that when he took office he decided that the first step was to wipe out those debts.
I do not cite that historic illustration for the purpose of saying simply, as many do, that the only thing to do now is to wipe out debts. It is not as simple as that. I could enlarge on this theme more fully, but I intend only to state one thing just as a sort of reminder that it is not as simple as it may appear, and that is this: The debts of many people to-day are represented on the other hand, by the savings of people equally deserving. For instance, the savings of estates which are the support of widows and orphans, and so forth, invested through trust and loan companies constitute the debts of people who are the mortgagors and the borrowers. It is not enough to say that debts should be wiped out; one must follow the thing through and recognize the injustices which might be done by a sweeping reform of that character. Nevertheless the fact remains that international debts are resting and bearing so heavily upon the people of the world as to constitute a problem which must be faced and for which we must find some relief or remedy.
I should like to discuss briefly the questions of currency and money as I think it is desirable to have some understanding of the elementary principles which underlie these terms. We use them very often quite thoughtlessly and glibly and fail to realize the important elements involved. From time immemorial the activities of man have been vitally influenced by money in some form or another. I hear certain economists-if I may so term them-say: Let us have barter, let us exchange some of the goods we have here for goods elsewhere. Or they say: After all, trade is nothing but barter. These loose utterances leave the impression that there is nothing involved but the exchange of wheat for silk, or something of that character. Trade is much more complex than that. As I say, from time immemorial money has been an important element in the exchange of goods and from the most exhaustive study I have been able to give to the question I believe it is useless to think of returning to the old system of barter unless we desire to revert to the old standards which obtained when barter was the sole process in the exchange of goods. Money has become a standard or measure of value. At this point may I emphasize this fact: One thing above all else is essential in money, and that is confidence.

I agree with that, too, so there is no point of difference between us. As I was saying, there is one thing above all else essential in money, and that is confidence. In other words it is quite useless for Canada, for instance, to have a certain type of money which might be quite satisfactory to us and sufficient to handle our internal business, if China, Great Britain, South America, South Africa or any other country would not accept it at its face value as money. The whole secret of the success of the use of money in the settlement for the interchange of goods is that there be confidence in the money used. I should like that point to be kept very clearly in mind.
Another point is this: Money in itself does not increase. There is, I think, a very widespread and false belief that money loaned out and bearing interest increases because of the fact that it bears interest. Money does not increase, the payment of that interest comes from some other source as the result of the production of goods of some kind by the people who pay the interest. In other words, money does not increase or accumulate except by the addition to it of interest which represents, in turn, production by the debtor.
The suggestion is made sometimes that commodities can be used as money or that money should be based upon commodities. I shall have more to say about this in a moment, but at this point I should like to say that from time immemorial, as far back in history as we can read, gold and silver have been largely the bases of money. Only recently I read a very interesting book dealing with the monetary system of China, which goes back to 1200 B.C. I was tremendously impressed with the fact that throughout the

centuries and millenniums that great country has been using money, chiefly in the form of silver it is true, but case after case is disclosed in that historic record where gold played a very important part. Only a few years ago a very definite effort was made to introduce a gold standard in China. I merely mention this in order to emphasize the fact that gold and silver have served humanity in a most valuable way and in a most important manner in the form of money.
I should like to give expression to a thought which may find response in the hearts of some but which may be considered to be heresy by others. This thought is:	Money
loaned for other than productive purposes constitutes a drain upon production, capital and the interest thereon double the burden upon production.

As I was saying, it was not until 1791 that bank cheques were introduced, and unquestionably they became a part of the currency of the realm, a secondary part. Undoubtedly they facilitate the movement of goods and the extension of industry and commerce. It should always be borne in mind that bills of exchange, drafts, cheques and so on are a most valuable adjunct-shall I say?-or support to a universal currency, but the usefulness and universality of this class of currency is limited by two considerations, the house upon which it is drawn, and the drawer of the instrument, whatever it may be. Of course, I admit this, that the Bank of Montreal, for instance, drawing a cheque on itself, would have that cheque accepted in almost any centre in the world, but a cheque drawn by myself on the Bank of Montreal would be perfectly useless outside the limited sphere in which I am personally known.
Another point I wish to make is this, that gold in so far as it is attached to currency, is undoubtedly very, very valuable for two things: One is the settlement of international accounts, whether for trade or for debts or whatever it may be, and the other as a background or basis of security for internal currency.
For a moment let me refer to this question of the sufficiency or otherwise of gold. I do not think so. I would rather not digress into a lengthy explanation to give my views on that point. Briefly, I would not agree to that being the case.
The production of gold now amounts to about S400,000,000 per annum. Roughly speaking, about half of this goes to arts and industries for various uses and in various forms. The other half goes into the currency. I am giving just rough figures. As I said a moment ago, it is estimated that the extension of trade generally throughout the world calls for an increasing use of gold as a basis of currency, and it is generally accepted that there is a shortage of about S100,090,000 for that purpose.
Another point I wish to emphasize is this. The gold system that we hear referred to is not a system which has been deliberately designed and put into operation. I think we make a tremendous mistake in discussing questions pertaining to economics in this house and elsewhere, when we refer to the gold system or the capitalist system as if it were something that had been taken and put into a finished form, something which could be removed and replaced by some plan or system without interfering with or to any great extent disturbing the forces of the nation.
The gold system has grown into the warp and woof of the financial, commercial and industrial life of the countries where it is being used. Unquestionably a departure from it, a correction or disturbance of it, whatever character those changes may take, must and will affect all the various units interested in the country where such a change is made. By that I am not for one moment suggesting that we should simply sit down and do nothing about the gold standard system-not at all. Recognizing, however, that there is an insufficiency of gold to uphold the system as it is operated to-day, and at the same time do justice to internal and international trade, we cannot say that by merely wiping out such a standard and replacing it by a paper system we will correct the evil complained of.

I shall come to that; I
am now speaking of paper currency. There are those who argue that all that is necessary is to issue a currency bearing the mark of a nation and bearing on it the statement, "This is a dollar bill, and is backed by the general credit of the nation." That may be a somewhat extreme view. At this point may I refer to, and compliment the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) upon his speech delivered a few nights ago. In my view it was, by long odds, the most informative speech delivered in this discussion this session. He did, however, refer to the investigation made by the banldng and commerce committee of 1923 and complained, at least to some degree, of the attitude of some hon. members on that occasion who opposed certain proposals, and to which group I belonged. One of those proposals was that we should turn on the printing presses, turn out two billion five hundred thousand dollars worth of dominion notes and pay off the bonded indebtedness of Canada, thus eliminating the necessity for paying interest. That was one of the suggestions to which at that time I took very sharp objection. I wish to point out now that simply by turning on the printing presses and producing currency we will not get money which will be of value in internal or international trade, because such money will then be accepted only upon the value placed upon it by those to whom it is offered in exchange for goods. Hon. members will recall that when Germany, Austria, Poland and other countries in Europe during the years following the war turned on their printing presses and issued great quantities of paper currency, the result was a race between the receiver of such currency and the person who parted with the goods as to who could reach the bank first, or could first get rid of the currency in exchange for other goods. So accelerating was this round of effort that the printing presses could not turn the money out fast enough. The result was commercial and industrial collapse.
Already I have dealt briefly with the matter of cheques and bills of exchange. Some argue that the only currency required would be bills of exchange which represent commodities. At this time I should like to refer to this angle of the question. It is quite true that a warehouse receipt for 100,000 bushels of wheat is a very valuable instrument and one which can be used in exchange for something else. For the sake of simplicity we will bring the number of bushels down to 1,000 so that it will TMr. Stevens.]
be within the ken of most of us. We will suppose that a man holds a warehouse receipt for 1,000 bushels of wheat which, we will say, is worth $1 a bushel. He has $1,000 in hand. However, he wants to pay $100 on his grocery bill and other bills which have been accumulating; he wishes to buy a plough; he wishes to buy clothing and food for use in his house. Probably there are a dozen things he wants to do. Our present procedure is to deposit the warehouse receipt in the bank and, through the agency of currency which is accepted by everybody at a fairly well stabilized value, that man goes out and buys the things he requires, and pays his debts. So that while we may admit that a bill of exchange representing commodities is, unquestionably, a useful piece of paper as currency, it is not a piece of paper which can be used with facility, or a medium through which trade can be facilitated throughout the world. Furthermore, we may suppose that a man who acquires a piece of this paper does not want to spend it all at once. Wishing to have it last for a period of six months he must be in a position to turn it into something with which, at will, he can buy other commodities. Again arises the absolute necessity of a currency universally accepted and one which can be used at will for purposes of replacement.
Of course it is highly desirable that there should be a degree of constancy in currency. The currency that a farmer, for instance, would receive for his wheat in the autumn which might be worth only half its value in the spring would certainly be a bad piece of currency. It is true that under the unusual and abnormal deflation of the past two years, that is precisely what has happened. A person, for instance, who put a mortgage on his farm two years ago when wheat was, we will say, $1.50 a bushel, received, we will suppose, about $1,500 in the currency of the time, and spent it for some purpose. To-day however he is asked to pay back that debt, and there will be required, roughly speaking, about 4,500 bushels of wheat to pay back a sum equal to the value of 1,500 bushels two or three years ago. Obviously something is radically wrong, and it is that defect we are trying to correct. What is required is a currency which will remain reasonably stable, a currency which will be universally acceptable and one which, as I said a minute ago, will not fluctuate from day to day or from month to month. Yet, those who advocate paper currency, are, I think, inviting the most fickle and most uncertain type of currency.
I should like to deal further with that point, but I must hasten on. Reference has been

Stabilization of Currency
made to a managed currency. In this respect I wish to say that from my observations, which during the past few years have been fairly intense, I have not yet heard a really clear definition of what is meant by "managed currency." Nearly everyone who speaks upon the subject uses more or less vague terms, and there is no precise definition of what is meant by managed currency. It would seem that one has one meaning, and another another. I have in my hand the Macmillan report from which I wish to read a brief extract concerning this particular subject. Discussing the question of managed currency I find the following:
It may be asked whether the aim of central bank policy should not be to return to the more automatic working of the gold standard of prewar days.
The central bank policy is, invariably, connected with managed currency. The general suggestion was that central banks should be erected in each of the major countries of the world-in fact, in all countries through whose offices the management or control of currency should be manipulated or performed. I repeat the extract from the report:
It may be asked whether the aim of central bank policy should not be to return to the more automatic working of the gold standard of prewar days.
I read that for one purpose only at the moment. Even this committee which leans strongly to a managed currency indicates that it is necessary to have a scheme that will work automatically. And that is really the main complaint that I have against any scheme of managed currency that is at present offered. The report continues:
. . . Both the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and the Bank of England have developed very considerably the "open market" system which has been found in certain respects extremely effective. It is in itself, however, the antithesis of an automatic system. Thus, we believe, all central banks are faced with the necessity of a greater "management" of their currency systems, involving inevitably greater responsibilities and also a more urgent need of cooperation.
Then they state the obstacle facing central banks, one of which I mow cite:
In this task of management the central banks are faced with possible divergences between the interests of their own country and those of the world outside.
That is the very point to which I wish to draw particular attention. A managed currency presupposes certain things. One is this, that a central bank organization, or a central financial organization, within a country which is enabled to control all banking therein will
be empowered so to control the loans that are made and the interest that is charged as to manipulate the currency in circulation up or down in order to maintain a balance between the currency in circulation and the requirements of trade for currency. That, roughly speaking, is what they are called upon to do.
But here is the fatal weakness, to my mind, in a managed currency within a country. It is necessary for the group of individuals who control that central bank or central financial authority to foresee what the needs may be one, two, three months hence, because these things cannot in their very nature be put into operation overnight; the effects of what is done to-day in the loaning or putting into circulation of money cannot possibly be known until a few weeks or a few months hence, and so it is necessary for the banks, or the controlling factor in this matter, to have a prescience that will enable them to see into the future what the possible effects of their action to-day may be.
Lett us look at what happened in the United States. The United States have what is called a managed currency. The Federal Reserve Bank system, through their open market operations and the raising and lowering of interest charges, are able to control the movement of currency in or out. What happened in 1929 when the stock boom was-Shall I say?-on the flood, when it was becoming alarming? They raised the interest on loans to brokers to 10 per cent, then to 15 per cent, and, if my memory does not fail me, to as 'high as 25 per cent. And yet, this did not correct the situation, it did not prevent the crash, it did not prevent hundreds of millions, yes, billions of dollars flowing into the wildest orgy of speculation the world has ever seen.
I am told my time is about up. I Should like a few more minutes on this point, Mr. Speaker.

I have said, I think,
sufficient on the difficulties of a managed currency internally. Then come to this: multiplied by the prejudices and the needs of forty or fifty countries, one can visualize the difficulty. For instance, a managed currency that would take in the United States, Great Britain, Germany, France and Italy would require, in the first place, that the central control factor in each of those countries was able to foresee the effect on currency of loans or of rates of interest within their own territory, plus being able to agree with the central authorities of each of the other coun-
Stabilization of Currency

tries as to what should be done to-day for what may happen three months hence. My own opinion is, and I have seen nothing to change it, that a managed currency presents the gravest of difficulties in its working out. If it does not work almost to perfection, then the object for which it is brought into exisfc-ence is defeated; for if there is a variation in the value of the currencies, then the very difficulty we are confronted with, the exchange difficulty, is present in just the same manner as it is to-day.
There is a fourth suggestion-a currency with a metallic basis composed of silver and gold. As I intimated a moment ago, one of the difficulties in connection with the gold standard, in which I think all the leading authorities are in agreement, is that there is insufficient gold in the world properly to sustain the gold standard and facilitate trade; that is, in its present form of use. Now, one of the reasons for that is that it is possible either for individuals or for countries to hoard gold. Gold is so valuable and of such small compass in proportion to value that it can be easily hoarded. It is a matter of history that countries, for instance, India and China, absorb tremendous quantities of gold. No one knows where it goes; it is simply absorbed and passes out of circulation and out of use; it is lost so far as the world and the services of industry and commerce are concerned. That is well known. It is hoarded because of its high value in comparison to other commodities. But, it is argued by some, if you had as the basis of your currency silver and gold, it would not be possible to corner or to hoard it; therefore you would create a currency the quantity of which would be automatically controlled by the general production of these two metals, that there would be no incentive to hoarding, and thus there would be a wide and general distribution. I am not going into a detailed analysis of the argument any further than to summarize my remarks in this way:	When we
enter into a study of currency questions I think it is advisable to keep in mind the need of a currency in which there is universal confidence, and that all the factors should be given most careful study and consideration. In offering this amendment we are inviting the house simply to pass on to the Imperial economic conference authority for the Canadian delegates at that conference to initiate and support measures that will bring about a careful and exhaustive study of this very important question.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR CONSIDERATION ON AGENDA OF IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I am speaking now with regard to the speech made and amendment moved by my hon. friend this afternoon. If there is one thing above another in connection with his address on which I might congratulate him it is the very manifest way in which he disclosed the fact that of all subjects, this question of currency is one of the most intricate and complicated. Having done that, I submit that 'before he asks parliament to authorize the ministry to initiate and support any measures respecting currencies, he should ,be in a position to state to parliament what that measure is so that we may pass upon it. Let the minister bring in a measure which he believes will have that effect, and let us debate it. We may find out that it will serve the end in view; on the other hand we may find out that it will be far from serving that end. My objection to the amendment proposed by the minister, in particular, is that it requests blanket authority to the ministry to propose any measure with the result that parliament will then be put in -the position that it has authorized the ministry to take the step it has.
I should like to point out another possibility; the minister may say this is not the intention of his resolution, but in considering resolutions we must be very careful as to their intent as expressed. The resolution states not only that the ministry shall initiate measures but that it shall support measures for the sta'blization of currency. If this method is to be followed, measures possibly will be brought before the conference having to do with the stabilization of currency which are expressive of the view's of India, of Australia, of New Zealand, of South Africa, of the Irish Free State, or of Newfoundland. Is this parliament to instruct the ministry in advance that they are to support any measures simply because they are labelled measures to assist in -the stabilization of currencies? The resolution as it reads is an instruction to the ministry at the forthcoming Imperial economic conference to support measures that have stabilization in view. Well, who is to determine whether a measure brought before the conference is or 'is not a proper one? I

say that an instruction of that kind is altogether too wide and too general. It would be a very serious mistake. I do not think it is a method which would commend itself to -any of the governments that might be present at the forthcoming economic conference.
The minister, in concluding his speech, gave a rather different interpretation of the meaning of the amendment from that which it bears on its face. He said that it was asking simply that a careful study should be made of the question by the conference. Had he so worded his resolution I would have been prepared to support it most cordially, but such is not the wording or the meaning. I think that is the form in which a motion of this kind should be framed. I believe that among the different subjects to be dealt with at the approaching conference should be this important question of the stabilization of currency, and in my opinion it will require as much thought and attention as can be given to it by those who may be present. But the part of the conference should be in the nature of a study. The conference itself could, as a result of such study, if it so desired, make recommendations to be submitted later on to the various parliaments of the British empire for adoption as they might, see fit. May I say to my hon. friend that, having attended two imperial conferences, I may presume to know something of the procedure that is followed at these gatherings; and in this I think I shall have the support of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), who holds a similar point of view for I have heard him present it in this house time and again. He has said over and over again-and	I support this	view-that
a conference is essentially what is implied by the term:	It is a bringing together of
groups from different parts of the empire to consider and discuss certain questions. But in no sense is a conference a cabinet or imperial council; in no sense is it a body to lay down policies for the empire. It is a body to consider, and consider very carefully, what it will be best to recommend to the respective governments represented at the conference. If we are authorizing the ministry to initiate and to support certain measures at the conference we are to all intents and purposes placing the ministry in the position where, when the conference meets, they will have to assert that they have instructions from this parliament to press forward a certain measure and ask that it be adopted by the conference. In my opinion, it is not wise that the ministry should be placed in such a position.

Speaking at this moment in illustration of the point I am making, may I say to my right hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) that if tomorrow we on this side should ask the government to follow a certain course with respect to the tariff or any other matter that might come before the conference, I am sure he would reply immediately, albeit it is not the course he himself has followed, that it is not the business of the government, before going into the conference, to be too definitely committed to any policy or obliged to present a particular point of view-that the government must be perfectly free when it is in the conference to consider all aspects of a situation as they may be presented from different sides.
I believe my hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) has drawn his amendment with the best of intentions. but I have no doubt that on reflection he will agree that it is open to the interpretation which I have just put upon it-namely, an authorization of the ministry to initiate measures of which this parliament has no knowledge whatever, and to press those measures at the conference as representing the views which the Canadian people, through their parliament, have instructed the ministry to put forward. The proposal, as we have it,-is also in the nature of an obligation upon the ministry to support other measures that may have that particular end in view, although we do not know what they are. And in the third place it introduces, in rather ambiguous terms, a reference to economic unity, which may be all very well provided that this house is agreed upon the significance and the meaning of the term, but which might prove to be the very opposite should there be at the conference any misunderstanding as to just what is implied. My hon. friend says that there appeared in the original motion the words, "if the empire is to become an economic unit." When I saw the original resolution and read those words in it, I asked the hon. member on this side of the house (Mr. MacLean) what they meant, and he told me they were purely hypothetical or parenthetical and did not commit anyone to anything. I said to him, with regard to the phrase, an economic unit, that the government had put forward some idea of the kind, and that if they had anything of that sort in view this phrase would be the feature of the resolution which the government would seek to have control the whole.

I am sure my hon. friend would be able to go on with anything that means nothing. My understanding of the expression, "the empire as an economic unit," is this. Those who support the economic unit idea hold to the theory that the empire is to become an isolated economic unit, that it should be so organized that it will be possible for the different parts of the empire to trade only or almost exclusively within the empire. They believe that this economic isolation will be 'brought about by a system of tariffs around the whole, which will be so high as to render impossible trade of any extent with the rest of the world. Those -of us who sit on this side are wholly opposed to making of the empire an economic unit in that sense, and I submit that we should not be called upon to support a resolution that lends countenance of support to the theory in that sense of an economic union or unit. As regards anything that will make for unity of the empire, anything that will promote the prosperity of the empire, we on this side are as heartily in accord as are hon. gentlemen opposite. We all want to see the empire united and prosperous, but our view as to how that unity and that prosperity can best be achieved diifers diametrically from that of hon. gentlemen opposite.
If my hon. friend presses his amendment in the form in which it now stands, I am afraid I shall have to oppose it, and I hope he will understand quite clearly my reason for so doing. Speaking generally, apart altogether from his resolution, I do not think that this house should be asked to authorize the government to initiate or support any measure of which the house has no knowledge whatever, and I might add of which the government itself at this time has no knowledge. Furthermore. it should not be asked to instruct the ministry to support measures at the economic conference merely because they relate to a particular subject. I am heartily in accord with the whole idea of currency questions being studied at the conference, and any substantial contributions which can be made by the Canadian ministry towards that end will be something which I am sure will be appreciated not only in this country but in all parts of the empire.

Our money economy is really no more than a refined state of barter.
Apparently there are sorn-e real economists who hold that view. They d'o not contend that we ex-change goods for goods directly but they say that money itself -is a means by which barter is made possible in our highly complicated society.

May I say very frankly and sincerely that his re-marks came to me as the most discouraging thing I have heard in -this house sin-ce I first -became a member. Personally, I have been looking to him for great things during -this session, I have been expecting the opposition to bring forward real, constructive suggestions for the remedying of the real danger which exists, not only to Canada but to modern civilization. This question of currency is recognized by the statesmen of all countries as being the most urgent to be considered, -but the leader of the opposition has not one single constructive thought -to offer. He endeavours to make his opposition as effective as possible in trying to prevent the consideration of this matter at the Imperial conference. I suggest to the leader of the opposition that with a question of this importance confronting -the -public mind, and in the face of economic conditions which exist in the world to-day, he should have spent his time last summer studying this matter and should have come to this house with a real policy and given real leadership in the carrying into effect of that policy.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR CONSIDERATION ON AGENDA OF IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter of the stabilization of the currency of the empire is undoubtedly one of very great importance. Few things have done more injury, using the word in a broad sense, than the action taken in Great Britain in going off the gold standard. As a matter of fact, it wrecked the financial structure of practically every country in the world except two, and the loss sustained by Canada and by other parts of the empire was very, very great.
The question of empire currency is not new. It has been discussed at every succeeding imperial conference, but no action has ever been taken nor have any definite results followed. During or prior to the war my attention was directed to the possibility of providing for a pound containing gold to the value of five dollars with the hope that a pound or pax, or whatever name might be given to it, might have circulation in every part of the empire at that value. That had nothing whatever to do with paper money nor has it anything to do with the matter that is now being considered by this house, namely, that direction be given to the government that there be placed for consideration before the economic conference to be held in this city the question of a stabilized currency. The right hon. gentleman I am quite certain was not serious in suggesting that it was possible in February to prepare and submit to this house an agenda for a conference that is to meet in July. Neither would the right hon. gentleman I think, if pressed, and asked to look back on past conferences, say that it had ever been the practice nor could it be the practice to lay before the House of Commons the details of proposals that would be made to the. conference.
The question now before the house as expressed in the subamendment of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) is virtually that the question of the stabilization of, empire currency be brought to the attention of the conference.

He read copiously from essays and statements and speeches and reports of eminent men, and he indicated clearly that he had not the least knowledge in the world of the subject matter of the resolution. I am not saying that offensively. That is a matter of fact that will be found by reading the record. The hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) introduced an amendment and made a speech which indicated that he had profoundly studied the
Stabilization oj Currency

matter, but at the end he used words which indicated that his views as to a sound currency were not in accord with those which I believe are held by a majority of the members of this house. Having in mind the very circumstance to which the right hon. gentleman has alluded, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has indicated as clearly as it is possible to indicate anything that there are great difficulties in the way of a stabilized currency. By a stabilized currency it is not, of course, meant that you are going to give a like value to every form of currency or that you are going to have the like terminology for every form of currency, but that you are going to endeavour to establish a stabilized currency in order that the very difficulties to which the hon. member for Prince referred, namely, the great fluctuations in exchange values, should be avoided. I think this house will agree that it is highly desirable that the ends sought should be attained, if possible, by this conference.
I agree entirely with what has been said by the right hon. gentleman that a conference has no legislative power; it has no executive power. It has merely the power to recommend to the respective governments that action along certain lines should be taken, and that has been the case since these conferences were commenced. Their conclusions were not in any sense binding, and no one knows that better than the right hon. gentleman opposite. He knows that as a very condition of these conferences being held, those principles were asserted, and this house is not bound by anything that may take place at a conference until this house has seen fit to agree to what is recommended. When the right hon. gentleman came back from the Imperial conference which he attended in 1926 I think he will be the first to say that nothing had been placed on the records of this house that indicated that the proposals that were there considered were to be considered. There is nothing upon the records of Hansard or the Journals of this house that indicated that the great questions that were then discussed were to be discussed.

There is no legislative power in the conference. It cannot bind the members of this house nor the Dominion government, nor can the members who for the time being represent the country at that conference. The prime ministers of some of the great dominions in the commonwealth have from time to time contended that it was rather unsound that only one party should be represented at the conferences, that rather the government of the day should be assisted by the leader of the opposition and that there should be a representation of parliament, rather than of the government, to speak for the country at the conference. But that view has not obtained, and it is not likely to obtain.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR CONSIDERATION ON AGENDA OF IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I am glad that the right hon. gentleman thinks that a sound view. He has always expressed that view, as did his predecessor in office. The principle upon which opposition has been made to that view is this, that the government of the day must assume responsibility for what is done at the conference. When it comes back to parliament and asks parliament's approval with respect to any particular item of business that may have been transacted at the conference or of any conclusions embodied in the form of legislation, the government must assume sole responsibility for its action, and risk its life upon the result if it pledges its position as a government in asking the support of the house to those proposals. That view, I say, the right hon. gentleman has consistently maintained, and that is the view which many other members of various parliaments represented at imperial conferences have from time to time maintained. I am bound to say I used to think that at imperial conferences it would be much better if all parties in the state could be represented. But in discussions that I have had since responsibility has fallen to my lot it has appeared that there might be difficulties to which the right hon. gentleman has in times past referred. Whatever there may be of value in it from an academic viewpoint, as a practical matter it need not now be discussed, for the government will accept responsibility. The government cannot bind Canada to any line of action beyond agreeing to submit to parliament, its own parliament, any questions upon which deliberations have taken

Stabilization of Currency
place and conclusions have been reached. That was so, for instance, with respect to matters that were considered in 1930. That was so in connection with the Merchant Shipping Act. The Merchant Shipping Act is highly technical legislation. It was discussed in the 1926 conference. It was discussed in 1929 by a group of experts, and certain conclusions were formulated. It was again discussed in 1930, and certain approvals were given. But Canada could not be bound until such time as this parliament enacted legislation based and founded upon the conclusions which had been arrived at at the conference,-or, variations from them, if this house did not desire to approve.
This resolution, as it stands, asks the House of Commons-directs, if you will; I will use as strong a term as that-directs that Canada's representatives at the next Imperial economic conference to meet in this city shall place upon the agenda paper, or shall initiate discussions dealing with the stabilization of empire currency.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR CONSIDERATION ON AGENDA OF IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE
speechtext: If the amendment is redrafted I am content to support it in those terms, but I cannot in other terms.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR CONSIDERATION ON AGENDA OF IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I shall proceed a step
farther. The statement is also made that if the initiation comes from some other quarter, not that Canada will be bound by what some other quarter suggests, but that the Canadian delegation shall support not the identical measure, but any measure which deals with the stabilization of empire currency-if initiated, for instance, by India, South Africa, or it matters not where. That does not however for a moment imply that we will support those views. But the very fact that the subject is thrown into the melting pot for discussion involves the fact that there will be a free expression of views by men from various parts of this empire as to the possibilities of stabilization of empire currency. It is in that sense that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has presented this matter to the consideration of the house.
This is a question dealing with currency and trade. What we are endeavouring to promote by every means in our power is that on one-quarter of the world's surface, including as it does many countries and a quarter of the world's population, we should, if possible, have a stabilized currency or a medium of expressing values for trade and exchange and, in the words of the right hon. gentleman, "trade being exchange," that these media, if you will, should have values not necessarily in the same terms, but that they
should have stable values for the purpose of facilitating the transaction of business and the advancement of trade. That is the position. The language of the amendment to the amendment, which I have not before me, but which I saw before it was moved by my colleague, endeavours to express that view.
It is gratifying indeed to find the right hon. gentleman expressing a desire to cooperate with the government in the success of the conference. I venture to say-and I hope he will not take my comment as being unduly unkind-that his remarks present a marked contrast with observations he made publicly elsewhere, in which the very fact that a conference would be held at all was called in doubt, when he was wondering if there ever would be one. The very name of the conference must indicate its character. It is to be an economic conference to deal with trade and currency, currency and trade, the development of them, the stabilizing, if possible, of our currency, a medium of exchange, or expressions of exchange values between the various parts of the empire- all these matters will be discussed. Whatever complaints may hereafter be made, whatever criticisms may be urged, and however doubtful the right hon. gentleman may have been in times past as to our ability to succeed in having a conference at all, we ought at least, it seems to me, to be entitled to some credit for having succeeded in our efforts. Whatever the conference may bring about, at least we have succeeded in our effort to secure one, and have had it definitely decided that such conference will be held in the capital city of Canada, where, most hon. members will recall, the second conference was held. The colonial conference of 1887 was succeeded by the conference of 1894 which met in the parliament buildings in this city. Those who are curious to see the matters then discussed, who are interested in the development of ideas, and realize that after all, a long time is required to make progress in any particular line of action, would do well, if they have some time at their disposal, to take from yonder library the records of that conference. They will find that there may be and, we hope will be, a realization in 1932 of the hopes, aspirations and views which found expression by the statesmen of the empire in 1894.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only a few very brief observations to make in this debate. It was my intention to enter upon a detailed analysis of the various factors brought into question by the motion of the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean), the amendment moved by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) and the subamendment now moved by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens). First, however, I should like to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) upon the, generally speaking, reasonable tone of the address he has just delivered. I wish also to offer to my hon. friend from Wetaskiwin the observation that, despite his obviously superior academic qualifications, there are some of us in the Liberal party who for years have given careful study and thought to the question of currency, and have advocated, as widely as he has, proper reforms in the Canadian currency system. Personally, having played some part in the publication of Liberal policies and theories, I repudiate the animadversions of the hon. member for Wetaskiwin.
I wish also to extend to the Minister of Trade and Commerce my personal felicitations upon his exhaustive and comprehensive analysis of the monetary situation. I think when he took his seat he received as much applause from the benches of the Liberal party as from his own side of the house. It is very encouraging to-day to find in the Canadian House of Commons a minister of the crown who has such a complete knowledge of the most intricate problems which concern us in Canada. Not speaking for the opposition, but only in a personal capacity, I wish it were possible at the coming Imperial economic conference for Canadians, regardless of their party affiliations, and leaving out of their discussions matters of tariff, to concentrate in more than a national manner upon the question of

currency reform. Because a significant feature about the Macmillan report to which reference was made a few nights ago and by the Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon, is that there is no mention in this brilliant report, presented to parliament by one of the most outstanding committees which ever functioned in the United Kingdom, of the possibility of an empire currency. Subsequent to the report of the Maomillan committee there was formed and established in the old kingdom a committee of the Federation of British industries and the Empire Economic Union. In paragraph 50 of the report of that committee there is a distinct recommendation in regard to the stabilization of empire currency. As the right hon. Prime Minister has just intimated, in previous conferences the question of currency reform was submitted by each dominion, and New Zealand brought it forward at the economic conference of 1923. I am convinced that the greatest danger facing Canada to-day is not the throbbing problem of unemployment, it is the imminent destruction of our social and economic system unless we wake up.
As far as I see the situation-and I am not speaking at all in a partisan sense

the remedies are twofold. In the first place, there are national remedies which can be applied by whatever government happens to be in offioe; in the second place, there are international remedies. And I am convinced that we cannot solve our weighty national problems except by international thought, international study and international discussion. That is the reason why the Macmillan committee has based all its observations in regard to monetary reform, not on the empire unit, but on the world.
I am exceedingly pleased to know that the question of currency will be discussed at the economic conference next July. I think that all parties in this house are united on that idea. Unfortunately we are divided on the phraseology of the motion and the amendment. Personally I am conscientiously opposed to the motion, and with my limited study of economic questions I am opposed to the amendment of the learned member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine). I am also opposed -but only as to phraseology-to the amendment so ably moved by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce and which now becomes a matter of government policy. We who are adhering to Liberal principles and to certain tariff doctrines are not forgetful that the phrase "economic unity," although it sounds glorious, has a sinister origin. I want to keep this discussion entirely non-partisan, but it

Stabilization of Currency
must not be forgotten that that was the slogan used by our good friend Lord Beaver-brook when he was proclaiming his gospel of empire free trade. If my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce had used any one of these phrases "economic prosperity," "economic well being," "economic welfare," I am confident that every member in this house would be 100 per cent behind him. I suggest that if unity in Canada and in this house is worth while we can very well agree upon the language used by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister when he said that the amendment moved by the Minister of Trade and Commerce means only that instructions be given to the government to submit the question of a stabilized currency to the next Imperial economic conference. I think every single member, regardless of his political affiliations, will support the right hon. gentleman in that interpretation. It would be a wonderful gesture if this house could send a united (resolution instructing the administration to submit to the approaching conference the subject of currency reform, and this unanimity could be brought about by changing the phraseology of the amendment moved by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce. I trust the necessary steps may be taken to this end, for I am firmly convinced that currency reform is one of the greatest problems confronting not only Canada but the whole civilized world at the present time.
