speechtext:
This article carries at its head the name of J. B. McLean. It says:
The Foreign Money Ring and the World Crisis
The present financial flurry is merely another incident, in the progress of the international money ring.
The story of this super-banking system has been covered from time to time. . . .
In effect, it has been shown that a group of Austrian-German-Duteh-Greek-born financiers years ago settled in England, then the world's financial centre, among a people rich in character, in good records and great wealth. These foreigners proceeded to exploit and debauch that country-its commerce, its banking, its industries and its public men and public servants.
And so on. I do not want to take time to read all this, but somewhere near the end of the article it states that the forced departure of Britain from the gold standard may be

the final act of that money ring which was described. Then I have a copy of the front page of the Financial Times for September 25, 1931. It says:
Departure from gold basis may prove real boon. Basic industries and tourist business should benefit from dollar discount.
Another column bears the heading:
Dollar discount should be great newsprint help.
If there is any industry in Canada, other than agriculture, that seems to need a little help it would appear to be the newsprint industry. I could fill several pages of Hansard with quotations from the press to prove that the departure of Britain from the gold standard was a boon to industry and, to a certain extent, improved the employment situation in that country. If Canada had been wise enough to abandon the gold standard a year ago Canada would have benefited very substantially in the same way. Apparently the policy being pursued by Canada at present is to keep our dollar as near parity with the United States dollar as possible, but perhaps before proceeding to elaborate that point I might say that Canada has not abandoned the gold standard because the government wished to abandon it; she has abandoned it in fact, if not legally, because she had not the gold to meet the demands of foreign investors.

speechtext:
If my hon. friend objects
to stabilizing Canadian currency again on the gold basis, on what basis would he stabilize it?

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR CONSIDERATION ON AGENDA OF IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I will come to that right
away, for the benefit of my hon. friend. Rather than give him my own ideas I should like to quote a man who should be regarded as an authority. I refer to Doctor J. P. Day, associate professor of economics at McGill university, who is reported as saying:
A country which abandons the gold standard will find its exchanges fluctuating, but it is at least relieved from worrying about an adverse balance of indebtedness, since the fluctuations of the exchange will look after that.
I should like to commend that to the attention of the Prime Minister, who thinks one of the great problems of this country is to balance our trade. Then Professor Day says:
The first immediate necessity is therefore to restore stability to the foreign exchanges. Does this mean a return to the gold standard? I should not like to say this is a totally impossible event, but I agree with a writer in the Economist who says it would be a nightmare if the treasury and the Bank of England had closed their minds to any other idea.

Stabilization oj Currency
Probably it would be a nightmare for us also if the Prime Minister closed his mind to any other idea.
For, after all a return to the gold standard would only leave the world where we were a year ago, still faced with a crushing burden of indebtedness and a price level that afforded no prospect of rising. Furthermore, it is very doubtful even if Britain could return to the old parity rate, whether other countries, and especially debtor countries, could.
Then he refers to a suggestion made by Professor Leacock that the pound should be stabilized on gold but that the number of grains of gold in the pound be reduced. I will not read that. Then Professor Day says:
What I should infinitely prefer to see is a sterling block of countries formed. The British monetary authorities would do all in their power-which they are probably trying to do but finding political faction extraordinarily hampering-to keep sterling at a steady purchasing power at home. Other countries renouncing gold would also keep their monetary units at a stable purchasing power and if these efforts were successful, the foreign exchanges would be stable too.
I think that is the only thing necessary, stable price levels in different countries; then the rate of exchange between those countries will remain fairly stable.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR CONSIDERATION ON AGENDA OF IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit me to ask him a question without annoyance? Surely he will admit that obligations payable in gold must thus be paid?

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR CONSIDERATION ON AGENDA OF IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I am not suggesting any
change in that at all. This writer says:
No foreign exchange rates would fluctuate except those of countries on the gold standard and these need not if they like to disregard gold and manage their currencies with a similar aim. Thus the whole world would be aiming directly at the stabilization of the purchasing power of monetary units instead of indirectly as it formerly did when the effort was to keep all currencies with a similar aim.
That is a much better principle on which currency should be stabilized than the gold standard, and I think a return to the gold standard is absolutely impossible unless it is done by reducing the number of grains of gold to the pound, as has been suggested by Professor Leacock and many others. That was only a suggestion; I do not want to commit Professor Leacock to that principle, but that is one way in which it might be done.
There is a splendid article in the Toronto Saturday Night of October 17, 1931, by Professor T. E. Gregory, of the London School of Economics, who says in effect that the gold standard exercised such pressure on the price levels as to imperil the standard itself. Finally it did break the gold standard and
made it impossible for the countries of the world to operate under it. It became impossible for England 'to stay on that standard, and when England abandoned it nearly all other countries followed suit. To-day only a minority of the so-called civilized countries maintain a pretence of being on a gold standard. Of the countries that are on the gold standard I believe the United States is the only one that is really living up to the standard, that is, paying out gold on demand. Even France, who holds such a large share of the world's gold, will not pay out gold on demand except in the form of $8,000 bars, and of course the ordinary person cannot pre-[DOT] sent legal tender to the extent of $8,000 in demand for gold. So that the Bank of France is relieved of the necessity of paying gold to private individuals. Recently, according to an article in the Financial Post, United States $20 gold coins have been selling in Paris for $24. Frenchmen anxious to secure gold coins for hoarding must now pay a premium of 20 per cent to get that gold, even in a so-called gold standard country.
Some of the newer economists are coming more and more to the belief that currencies can and should be stabilized without reference to gold, and I am very pleased to note that Dr. D. M. Marvin, economist of the Royal bank, in a speech delivered recently before the Canadian Club of Toronto, suggested that possibility. According to the report:
He saw the high price of credit in countries on the gold standard as the major cause of the depression and suggested trade would swing upwards when credit was obtainable at more reasonable levels.
He goes on to suggest that the currencies of different countries in the world might be stabilized, practically in the way proposed in the remarks of Professor Day which I have already read to the house. The following observations are significant:
Those countries no longer on a gold basis have means of controlling their own price level, although the machinery for doing so is not perfect and outside of Great Britain and Sweden there seems to be no great number of economists and banking authorities who have given consideration to this phase of the subject. Generally, the attitude of the governments, the press and the public is that a misfortune has overtaken the country which will be overcome at the earliest possible moment. They overlook the advantages which have accrued to them by reason of the premium on gold and fail to realize that they can afford to seek the old parities of exchange with the gold countries only after deflation has been arrested and reversed and the price level of the gold countries brought up to a level with their own. . . . It would seem that the monetary loss to one class, mainly government bodies, will be somewhat more than offset by the gain of another

I
should like to take the opportunity which the subamendment gives me to say a few words with reference to the very able speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens). First of all I wish to congratulate him very heartily upon the splendid speech he made to the house this afternoon. There are one or two remarks of his to which I wish to refer, and if the rules of the house do not permit the minister to reply on this occasion I hope that he will do so at the next opportunity when the subject comes up, which I hope will be this session.
If I heard him correctly, he stated "That money itself is not increased". I would ask him to define what he terms money. Does he include in money not merely coin but currency and credit or anything that functions as money? If he includes all those three, and if I am correctly citing his statement that money itself is not increased, I cannot understand how he comes to his conclusion, when every time we make a new issue of coins at the mint we are certainly increasing the quantity of money, and every time the banks take avantage of their power of note issue currency is certainly increased. Currency is increased every time the banks use the Finance Act provisions which enable them to bring various securities to the treasury board and to get dominion notes. Also in time of war, as in 1914, when our circulating medium was increased by about two billion dollars, surely money was increased. In this connection I would refer to a statement made by Sir Thomas White in his book, War-time Finance, in which he said that Canada surprised not only herself but the whole world when her people subscribed twice as much money as all the money in Canada to various war loans, and then had amply sufficient in addition to carry on a growing business. I would like the Minister of Trade and Commerce to be kind enough to answer those questions when he rises the next time this subject is under debate.
Secondly, he referred to a managed currency. I would ask him if by that he meant currency and credit, because currency itself is a very small part of our monetary medium.
Stabilization oj Currency

Thirdly, he referred to someone in the banking and commerce committee of 1923 advocating the very free issue and printing of paper money. I would remind the house that no one in this corner during the last ten years to my knowledge has ever for a moment suggested using the printing machines for issuing money without any check whatever. We have always been very, very careful to guard against such a policy.
Before I sit down I wish to refer briefly to a remark that was made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) this afternoon. He informed the house that the Liberal party had for some time past been giving a great deal of study to this monetary question. I am fully aware that the hon. member himself has been giving some study to it, but except for a few words that he uttered on a previous occasion I had never heard a speech made on this subject by any member of the party to my right until the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) spoke the other evening. But if it is true that the party to my right is making a serious study of the money question, I wish to say most sincerely that it is one of the best pieces of news that we have had for a long time, and anything that I and those sitting around me can do to cooperate with them in studying this all-important subject we shall be only too glad to do at any time and place.

Mr. Speaker, owing to the indisposition of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), lam, for the moment, content to take his place rather than to ask the hon. member to let his bill stand. During recent years, having regard to the decisions of the courts, I think there have been relatively few violations of the provisions of the Bank Act, as compared with conditions prior to the first decision of the courts as to the legality of charging more than 7 per cent. I agree wholly with what the hon. member has said, that laws placed upon the
statute books should be observed whether by corporations or by individuals. They are intended for both and should be respected equally by each; as to that I think there can be no doubt.
There are, however, reasons given by the chartered banks why in some communities they have, as a matter of contract, charged more than 7 per cent; they said if they did not do so they would have had to close their branches. May I add that they have given lists of communities in which that fact is true. Whether or not those reasons would satisfy the hon. member and his friends as to the soundness of the position which has been taken, I am not prepared to say. All I can say is that last year, as he has very properly pointed out, the penalties were out of all proportion to the offences. To-night if I were going to criticize any particular section of this bill-and I do not purpose to discuss it at length-I would say that to make a violation of the act an indictable offence would involve the provinces in very large expenditures of public moneys for prosecutions and, in most instances, I should fancy there would be difficulty in securing convictions. A summary conviction would probably be sufficient to meet all the purposes the hon. member has in mind. Without in any sense committing myself to the principle that he suggests, but agreeing wholly with him that any law placed upon the statute books should be observed, I suggest to him that if he will, without committing hon. members to the principle of the bill, let the house give it its second reading, it can be referred to the committee on banking and commerce, where an opportunity will be afforded to those who are interested to express their views and fully present the case which they may make as to the undesirability of enacting a clause such as suggested so long as banks are asked to be maintained in very small communities where the cost of maintenance is far beyond the profits derived from their operation. If the hon. gentleman is prepared to adopt my suggestion, I would certainly commend that course to the house.

Mr. A. U. G. BURY (East Edmonton) moved the second reading of Bill No. 17 to amend the Marriage and Divorce Act.
Marriage and Divorce Act
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think
there is much that I can add to the explanation I gave the house when asking leave to introduce the bill. The amendments are of a very simple nature. The marriage law as it now stands provides that a man may marry his deceased wife's sister or the daughter of a sister . of his deceased wife, but does not provide that he may marry the daughter of a brother of his deceased wife. The first amendment is for the purpose of making it legal for a man to marry the daughter of a brother of his deceased wife, as he may now marry the daughter of a sister of a deceased wife. The second amendment is analogous to that in reference to the woman. By the marriage law of Canada a woman can marry now a brother of her deceased husband, or the son of a brother of her deceased husband, but cannot marry the son of a sister of her deceased husband. The second amendment is for the purpose of remedying this anomaly.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. W. KENNEDY (Winnipeg South Centre):
subtopic: EXCLUSION OF OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OF ACT.
speechtext:
I wish very briefly to further discuss certain details of this bill. When speaking to the bill the other day the hon. member for Bow River (Mt. Garland) drew the attention of the house to the fact that if it were enacted it would have the effect of destroying what is ordinarily known as the preference under the Civil Service Act to those who served in His Majesty's forces overseas during the war. If there be any doubt as to the force of the point raised by the hon. member, reference to the act itself will make the position very plain. Section 26 of the Civil Service Act provides:
Competitive examinations shall be held by the commission to establish lists of persons eligible for appointment.
Section 29 contains this provision:
Immediately after each examination a list of ;he successful competitors in the case of a competitive examination, and of successful candidates in order of merit in other examinations, shall be made out and published in the Canada Gazette.

2. The commission shall prepare and maintain a special list of persons in receipt of pensions by reason of their services in the war who
(a)	have from causes attributable to such service lost capacity for physical exertion to an extent which makes them unfit efficiently to pursue the avocations which they were pursuing before the war;
(b)	have not been successfully reestablished in some other avocation; and
(c)	desire to be placed on such list.
There provision is made for a special list on which shall be placed those in receipt of pensions who have qualified at competitive examinations. Section 29 provides further by subsection 4:
In all examinations for entrance into the civil service the persons named on such special list who are found to possess the necessary qualifications shall be named, in the order of merit, on the list of successful candidates above all other candidates; and all other persons who have been on active service overseas on the military forces or who have served on the high seas in a seagoing ship of war in the naval forces of His Majesty, or of any of the allies of His Majesty, during the war, who have left such service with an honourable record or who have been honourably discharged,, or when any persons who have served as aforesaid have died owing to such service, the widows of such persons, and who, in either case, obtain sufficient marks to pass such examinations, shall, irrespective of the marks they have obtained, be named in the order of merit, on the list of successful candidates next after any candidates who are on the special list mentioned in subsection two of this section and above all other candidates.
This bill provides that section 63 be added, as follows:
The outside service shall be excluded from the operation of the act, and the governor in council may make such regulations as are deemed advisable, prescribing how such positions are to be dealt with.
It is obvious that the only preference with respect to those who served overseas, so far as appointments to the civil service are concerned, is created by virtue of and under the provisions of the Civil Service Act. Therefore if all outside appointments be removed from the operation of the Civil Service Act, certainly the provisions of that act will no longer apply thereto.
In fairness to tlhe hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon), who introduced the bill, I wish to state to the house that I have had the privilege of talking over the matter with him. He informs me, and certainly I am convinced, that it was never in his mind that the proposed amendments to the Civil Service Act should destroy that preference. But in addition to being generously endowed by nature with a keen mind, the hon. member has the further advantage of a training in law and a mature experience, so I think no

Civil Service Act-Mr. Kennedy (Winnipeg)
argument is necessary to convince him-and I assume it will not be necessary bo convince other hon. members of this house-that we must take the bill as we find it. It is true that the bill itself makes no reference to the removal of such preference, but in connection with the removal of outside appointments from the Civil Service Act it makes no reservation in relation to the preference at present enjoyed. Therefore, whatever may have been the intention, we must face the facts as they are, and if the bill were passed in its present form it would have the effect of destroying that- preference.
It is not my purpose to-night to enter into any discussion or argument as to whether or not such preferences should have been granted. That question is not before the house. But the effect being as I have indicated, for that reason alone I cannot support the bill. It is true that the measure contains a provision that with respect to apointments to the outside service the governor in council may make such regulations as are deemed advisable, yet the bill itself contains no reference to what those regulations may be, so I cannot give it my support.
That is only one feature of the bill, though it is an important feature. In their general application, however, other provisions of the bill are much wider. They refer to all appointments to the outside service, that is to say, to all appointments outside the city of Ottawa and its immediate environs. It means that with respect to all outside appointments we are going back to the patronage system. Was it not an advance when the Civil Service Act was introduced? I am indebted to the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland), who has placed on Hansard extracts from the speeches of distinguished members of this house relative thereto. The fact that they are there makes it unnecessary for me to repeat or refer to them in detail, but the general feeling was that in the interests of the public service it was advisable that so far as possible we should do away with the old system of patronage.
Were those men wrong? I am aware of the fact that in the administration of the act the Civil Service Commission cannot be held blameless, in view of certain recent investigations and exposures. But because that is so is it desirable that we do away with the whole operation of the act? Surely it is a question of the proper administration of the act, and not a question of doing away with the principle on which it is based. If in their administration of the aot the present Civil Service Commission have allowed considerations other than merit to enter into the question of appointments; if they have allowed considerations other than merit to enter into the question of promotions, the fact remains that whether it be necessary to perform a minor or a major operation in connection with the commission, this is a matter of disciplining that body. I understand that a committee of this house is to be appointed to consider the whole matter of the administration of the Civil Service Act by the commission; I understand from my hon. friend from Dorchester that it will be proposed that this bill be not pressed but that it be referred to a committee, so I am quite content that the matter should be disposed of in that way. I think it is desirable in the interest of the public service and of the administration of the Civil Service Act that the whole matter of its administration be thoroughly and diligently investigated by a committee of this house.
To take from under the operation of the act all appointments to the civil service of Canada outside of Ottawa is to my mind unthinkable. Instances have been given of appointments made under the Civil Service Commission as it operates to-day which have not been creditable, but to my mind those reflections have not been upon the principle but rather upon the administration of the act.
I have heard it urged that hon. members know best who should be appointed from their constituencies. The other evening in discussing this bill I had occasion during the few minutes at my disposal to make reference to that phase of the matter. Frankly, I am not apprehensive to any great degree on that ground so far as original appointments are concerned, but assuming that original appointments, even if left in the hands of individual members, are made on merit, what about the uncertainty of the service if the principle of patronage is to apply? Take a young man in private industry. He enters the service of a firm with high hopes, willing to give of the best that is in him, expecting-what?-that by diligence, by industry and by the application of such abilities as he possesses he will get advancement. But once you introduce again into the civil service of Canada the principle that appointments shall be made on the strength of party service, there follows as day follows night this fact, that when there is a change of government those who owe their appointments to their party loyalty and party service will in many cases stand in danger of losing those appointments. The same principle would apply to either party; unfortunately it is too true. And with what result?

Civil Sendee Act-Mr. Aheam
The class of applicants you will get for positions in the service will deteriorate. What young man, ambitious and desirous of advancing himself in life, would wish to join the service knowing quite well that after probably eight or ten, or at the most twelve or fifteen years, he is going to face, to put it mildly, the possibility of being removed from the service? Apart from the deterioration in the class of applicants who would enter the service, consider the situation of public servants working under such conditions, with the apprehension always ahead of them that some day diligence, industry and ability will avail them nothing but that instead, by virtue of the patronage principle, they may be cast out.
To my mind, apart altogether from the first observations I made in regard to the question of preference to returned men, it would be a mistake to pass the bill. I heartily endorse, however, the suggestion that a committee be appointed, that the whole question of the administration of the act be investigated and that helpful suggestions looking to its improvement be there fully considered.

I wish to make some very' brief remarks respecting the bill now before the house. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) and the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Kennedy) have left me very little to say because I find myself in almost complete agreement with both. I cannot regard this bill as anything but a very long step towards a return to the patronage system, and in my opinion the patronage system is as dead and as much discredited to-day as when it was abolished and the merit system, under the Civil Service Commission, substituted for it.' I do not believe that any case has been made out against the merit system. If there is any serious criticism it is directed against the Civil Service Commission and its methods; but those who believe in the merit system have no fear that a committee of this house, taking evidence in the fullest manner, can fail to point out a way to administer the merit system to the complete satisfaction of the people of this country.
I strongly believe that it is the will of the great majority of the Canadian people that entrance into the civil service of Canada shall be open to any Canadian who possesses the qualifications necessary for the position that he or she aspires to, and that adherence to any political party shall not be a consideration.
I believe that this is the great point insisted upon by the majority of Canadians, and that most hon. members on returning to their

constituencies will find that this feeling is just as strong to-day as it ever was.
I think I am safe in saying that those who are in the civil service stand almost as a unit in opposition to the provisions of this bill-The merit system, to those who have got into the civil service, stands as a guard against favouritism and influence, which I believe would endanger them if the patronage system were restored. Civil servants giving faithful and honest service would lose all feeling of safety, security and fair play.
A man may be a good and efficient party worker but at the same time be utterly unsuited to some position in the civil service which he may aspire to. Yet, frankly, I feel that hon. members would find it difficult to resist pressure from party organizations to recommend that type of man under certain circumstances. My own opinion is that patronage is a snare and a delusion so far as any member of parliament is concerned. You recommend one man for a position and immediately you incur the hostility of ten or twelve others; and you find yourself, so far as your own party is concerned, in greater difficulty than if you had done nothing at all. For that reason, looking at it from the point of view of practical politics, I do not think there is anything to be said for patronage.
I hope and expect that this bill now before the house will be defeated, and if that occurs the committee proposed by the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) will be appointed. In that event the Civil Service Commission will appear before the committee and tell its side of the story-because there are always two sides to any story. Until that examination is completed, and findings based on evidence are arrived at, I do not propose to criticize the Civil Service Commission in any way.
A certain amount of political patronage affecting minor jobs still flourishes, unfortunately. I regret to say that a letter from a ward chairman, a member of parliament or a defeated candidate is still as potent to-day as it has been in the past. Nothing has hurt the people of my own constituency more than the fact that, in these hard times, those who are in need of help cannot obtain assistance. I think we should consider ourselves as Canadians first and party men afterwards.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy indeed to associate myself with those who have preceded me and to say that I stand four-square in favour of the merit system. I have a good many civil servants in my constituency who have given faithful and diligent service to the crown. After serving a number of years and after buying property and entering into numerous obligations on the strength of a permanent position, they might find themselves on the street and their families placed in very painful circumstances
I believe in the merit system, I think it is the fairer way of making appointments, and in the long run it is productive of the best results. It is also more satisfactory for the employees themselves. After giving many years of faithful service it is only fair that they should obtain the promotion to which they are entitled. Under this system the employees

I do not think the member for the district in which an appointment is to be made should be entirely ignored. After all, the member should have some say as to who should be appointed. He is as a rule a person of reasonable intelligence, and more than that, he is the choice of the people of the district. Surely, therefore, he should have some voice in the selection of those who are to carry on the business of the government in the riding that he represents. The inside service is not under consideration in this connection at all, but when there is a vacancy in the outside service, what happens at the present time? There is a perfunctory kind of examination; some representative of the department concerned, I suppose, goes down to the district, probably knowing nothing of it or of the candidates, and after making a few cursory inquiries goes back and reports to the Civil Service Commission that such and such a person is the one he thinks should be appointed to the position. He has not the means of knowledge which are open to the member for the district, because generally the member has been brought up in that district and is very well acquainted with the people who are likely to be applicants. So I submit that the committee should consider this question; that after a list of eligible candidates has been prepared by the commission it should be submitted to the member for the district, or at least the first three or four names on the list, so that the member may express his opinion as to the merits of the candidate. In that way we would

avoid having someone appointed who is not really under all the circumstances the most suitable person for the position. I think the member can be relied upon to select a suitable candidate. He is responsible to the people he represents, and I am sure he can be relied upon to decide on the basis of merit.

I suppose there is very little to be gained in prolonging the debate after the announcement by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) that he proposes to appoint a committee to inquire into the administration of the Civil Service Act and possible changes that may be made in it, but I should like to state my own view that it would be a backward step to make any drastic change in the principle of the Civil Service Act.
I am at a loss to know whence come the objections to the act. Perhaps I should not put it in that way. So far as I can ascertain, there has never been any great objection on the part of the Canadian people to the purpose and operation of the Civil Service Act as it is to-day. The objections come almost entirely, I believe, from individual members of the House of Commons, who seem to believe that they are in a better position to make these appointments than the members of the Civil Service Commission. There may occasionally be some truth in that statement, but as a general principle I think it is absolutely incorrect, because with the best of intentions- I give credit to most, in fact all, of the members of the house for a desire to discharge their public duties with absolute honesty-it is entirely unavoidable if you return to the system of political patronage that the pressure will be so great that the chief thing to be observed in making recommendations to the Civil Service Commission will not be the merit and ability of the candidate to perform the duties of the office, but rather whether he has performed the right kind of political service for the party involved.

Not necessarily, but I am
afraid that that will be the case in very, very many instances.
The Civil Service Act was enacted, if I remember correctly, in 1918, under the Union government, as it was known. I think it has worked fairly well, although in 1921, again if I remember correctly, there was an attempt made to drive what was known then as a coach-and-four through the Civil Service Act by what was known as the Spinney bill. I happened to be a member of the committee to which the Spinney bill was referred, and I

Civil Service Act-Mr. Bennett
opposed the recommendation made by the committee at that time. In that recommendation was a clause to the effeot that the Civil Service Commission should have the power to divest itself of authority to appoint certain employees to the civil service if they regarded such action as being in the public interest. I hope that no such recommendation will be made by the committee which is now to be appointed, because that would transfer authority from parliament to its creature, the Civil Service Commission. If any changes are to be made, they should be made by parliament itself.
I am not here to say that there are not difficulties in the administration of the Civil Service Aot. After an operation of some thirteen or fourteen years I think it quite likely that changes in the act could be made with advantage to the service. Possibly I might be able to point out some myself. The statement has been made at times that one result of the enactment of the Civil Service Act as it is to-day has been to transfer the patronage from the members or the ministers to the heads of branches in the departments, and it may be that that has sometimes been the case. I can conceive of cases where the heads of branches, to whom after all is committed the giving of the ratings where promotions are concerned, may, if they do not do their duty, exercise favouritism either on political or on personal grounds. I am almost certain that that at times has been done and that in isolated instances favouritism or patronage has been exercised by the head of a branch rather than by the minister himself. But despite any weaknesses that may exist in the operation of the act, I still hold that the advantages to be gained by the provisions of the act are so much greater than any defects there may be, that there is really no argument with regard to the matter. There may have been difficulties, there may have been disadvantages, there may have been abuses in the administration of the act. If so, they should be disclosed before the committee.
It seems to me that there is a good deal of money wasted to-day. For instance, tonight I received in my mail notice of an appointment to be made to the wardenship of one of our penitentiaries. It is pretty much a waste of rime and money to print and distribute these notices. We receive them almost daily at home, and they are of absolutely no use to anybody. That practice might just as well be discontinued, because we have nothing whatever to say in the making of the appointments. I have a certain
degree of sympathy with the member for West Peterborough (Mr. Peck) when he says that the member might very well be consulted by those making inquiries in his neighbourhood as to appointments to certain vacancies. I can see no particular objection to that so long as there is no duress or compulsion, so long as the member is not clothed with any authority to dictate to those making the investigation.
I am entirely opposed to the principle of this bill and l am absolutely in favour of the amendment which will refer to a committee the matter of investigation and possible amendments to the act.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXCLUSION OF OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OF ACT.
speechtext:
I have heard observations made by hon. gentlemen opposite with respeot to the position I have frequently taken in connection with civil service appointments. I have advocated the merit system on more than one occasion in this house and out of it. During the last fifteen months I have had occasion to examine the operations of the statute, and I think perhaps this house is overlooking the fact that after we concede the merit system is the proper system, the next question is: Who is to determine merit? That is where the difficulty has arisen, and it is a real difficulty.
Let me give this house an illustration: In a certain town of this dominion it was necessary to appoint a caretaker for a public building. A representative of the Department of Public Works met the applicants and, having seen them and discussed their qualifications, placed one of them in charge temporarily. That man, had, first, the qualification of being a returned soldier; secondly, he had had some experience in the sort of work required; thirdly, he was of proper age, and lastly his scholastic attainments consisted of a public school education. He wrote the application in his own handwriting. There were other applicants for the same position; they, too, wrote their applications in their own handwriting, as required; at least some of them were returned soldiers. The temporary employee was rated by the public works examiner as being better qualified for the position than anyone else. Suddenly however an educational test became necessary for the job of caretaker, and a clerk in this city was named to determine the educational qualifications of the applicants. Without seeing them, and without any examination other than looking at the application forms which they had filed, he gave an applicant other than the one who was temporarily in charge eight points more than

Civil Service Act-Mr. Bennett
that temporary employee. The result is that the temporary appointee was put out of his position, and the appointment was given to the one who had the educational qualifications determined in his absence from looking at his application form; and mark you, the selection was made not by the Civil Service Commission but by a clerk who receives compensation I think wholly in keeping with his merits, and who was appointed for reasons which need not be discussed.
There you have the merit system; there you have an instance where the merit of that caretaker was determined by a clerk in Ottawa who never saw the applicants, and who determined that the educational qualifications of the one appointed were superior to those of the unfortunate young man who was in charge, who was also a returned soldier and who had as good an education, I would say -because I have photostatic copies of the original documents-as the one who succeeded in securing the position.
It must be apparent therefore that something must be done by which the merits of contending applicants may be decided by pioper methods. It was that case and other cases of the same type which made me so desirous of having this matter considered by a committee. We are shocked when we think of a man giving absolute satisfaction in a position, and who is actually better qualified by experience, being removed from it because, after looking at two application forms and without seeing or examining the applicants in any way, the educational test of one is said to be superior to the other.
I am now advised by the commission that the educational test has been removed in connection with positions of that kind. The result is that if that unfortunate returned man now had his position he would be able to keep it, but because attention was directed to this abuse he is now out of a position and another man who was not seen by the examiner and was given a rating of eight points higher than his competitor, on educational qualifications, is now working. I am bound to say that very ugly rumours were about as to what determined the difference of eight points; I leave them out, however, as they have nothing to do with the matter under discussion, I merely mention the circumstance.
Matters such as that have brought suspicion and distrust to the minds of many people concerning the commission, and have necessitated action being taken. Only the other day complaints were made as to the high expense of its operation. We gave notice to

that branch of the public service, as we did to others, concerning temporary employees. To-day we are advised that they can effect retrenchment to the extent of $9,000 per annum by the withdrawal of a certain number of temporary employees. That represents the interest on only $180,000, but indicates clearly why the public outside of Ottawa has become so deeply interested in what factors determine merit. I could recite a great many more cases of a similar character. Mistakes will happen; we must allow for them. Difficulties have to be overcome by experience in the operation of a statute. The present statute has been in force thirteen years, and the circumstances to which I referred happened only last year. As I say, there are others just like it. It is for that reason the government has concluded it owes a duty to the merit system to see that the factors which determine merit are factors not under the control of a hidden hand which operates through an official drawing an insignificant compensation, and with power to determine the life or death, officially, of applicants for positions. It is for that reason the government asks that this bill be referred to a committee so that these matters may be considered.

subtopic: EXCLUSION OF OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OF ACT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened attentively to the speeches of the members who preceded me in this debate. Some were in favour of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) requesting this house to amend the Civil Service Act by excluding the outside service, others, perhaps for personal reasons, express contrary views and oppose the bill.
In no manner do I wish to criticize the Civil Service Commission! Far be it from my thought, because I feel certain that in the discharge of their duties they have acted honestly to the best of their ability and in the interests of the public. However, I wish to state-even at the risk of shocking the house-that the Civil Service Act rests on a false principle, that is deceit. It was framed with a view of depriving members of both present and future governments of the responsibilities inherent to the administration. I state that the act is contrary to the principle of self-government, because a government conscious of its responsibilities must be vested with the authority necessary to appoint its officials or employees.
Far from being opposed to the merit system, I should like to see all applicants for positions in the public service, submit to the required tests; however, I would insist

Civil Service Act-Mr. Denis
that these examinations be corrected by those who are responsible for the administration, by those who are accountable to the people, and thereby best suited to choose, among the applicants, candidates who are as well qualified as those chosen by the present commission.
I am therefore in favour of the bill because it is in keeping with the principle of selfgovernment, and, because, notwithstanding the Civil Service Act, former governments as well as this government, have always managed to find positions for their friends. When the question of promotion arises, the heads of departments, for instance, are requested by the Civil Service Commissioners to report as to the qualifications required by the candidates, and I may state that often, under previous governments and the present one, favouritism was shown on such occasions to friends of the government which happened to be in power. Bearing in mind our responsibilities as legislators, we should avoid deceiving the electorate and enact legislation based on sincerity and honesty of purpose, so as to satisfy everybody and also in the best interests of Canada.
I therefore again state, sir, that this act is unjust-not to say hypocritical-and has but one aim, that of deceiving the members of Parliament and the candidates who aspire after civil service positions. In closing my remarks, I again state that I am in favour of this bill, however, I would not support it if I thought it had been introduced in order to reestablish patronage in the civil service. I believe in the sincerity of the sponsor of this bill and I am convinced the merit system will be retained in the administration of the civil service.
Instead of applying this system "at large" as at present, it should be applied in each department in such a way that the civil employees would be fairly dealt with, not be disappointed in their rights and not be dismissed for trivial reasons, like a large number of postmasters have been since this government is in power.
An hon. MEMBER (Translation): Do not forget that under the late government dismissals also took place.

speechtext:
For these
reasons, sir, I am in favour of the principle of the bill, and I trust that in the future this government, as well as the government which will, I am certain, replace it in two years, will have the right to appoint its employees in keeping with a merit system which takes into account the government's responsibility towards the people.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. U. G. BURY (East Edmonton):
subtopic: EXCLUSION OF OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OF ACT.
speechtext:
Whatever sentiments, Mr. Speaker, we may individually entertain towards either the bill under discussion or the motion which was moved by my friend from Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon), I think we can all agree that they have both served a good purpose in bringing up for discussion on the floor of the house, and we hope for some practical settlement, a question that has been-not to use a more inelegant term-long over-ripe for settlement. It is a question of very great importance to the public service of the dominion. I hope that the amendment which has been moved by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) will carry the support of the house. Not that I believe that it is the best way of dealing with the matter, but because it is a step in the right drection and maj'' enable us later to take a further step.
The questions raised and the issues involved in the bill itself and in the resolution affect the interests vitally and profoundly of a large body of our fellow citizens, many of whom have devoted practically all the active years of their life to the public service, and some of whom have built up a record for industry and effective and honest work of which any nation might well be proud. But those questions and issues concern not merely this great body of public servants, but the public service as a whole and the interests of the dominion. Therefore it seems to me that parliament can do nothing less than give to them the most serious consideration, the most searching inquiry and the strictest nonpartisan and patriotic thought.
When the hon. member introduced his resolution he ventured the assertion that he was assured of the support of nine-tenths of the members of the house. I doubted it at the time, but I said to myself:	Well, if that be
true, I am one of the twenty-four and a half members who constitute the one-tenth. I may be only the half member of the despicable minority, but I can take no other stand than I now take. I find, however, during the course of this debate that my hon. friend grossly exaggerated the amount of sympathy and support this resolution would evoke, and if I am any judge of the sentiments of the house I am quite satisfied that the resolution moved by the Minister of Justice will carry.
There were two .propositions put forward by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario from which I wish at once to dissociate myself. He said that the present act, the present civil service system, was a relic of war hysteria, that the parliament of 1918 was stampeded into taking up a position which was extreme,

Civil Service Act-Mr. Bury
which it never should have adopted, and from which we must now retreat. It may be that there is a certain measure of truth in the fact that war sentiment had its effect upon the measure introduced in 1918; it would have been unnatural if that had not been the case. Men felt profoundly at the time. But, Mr. Speaker, while we may give the greatest possible weight to the argument that postwar sentiment played its part in determining the provisions of the bill and the nature of the civil service system set up by the act, this argument has to do with details and not with the principle of the act itself. As I listened to the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon), I could find nothing in his speech dealing with the principle of the system or of the act, though I did find much that dealt with the administration of the act and with details.
If that be true, and if the controversy to-day has to do with details and not with orinoiple, does it not rather savour of a too drastic remedy to suggest that we should sacrifice the principle in order to rectify the details? Is it not a little like proposing to cut off Cromwell's head in order to remove his wart? We remember that the Protector had pretty strong views as to how he should be treated. He said to Lely, the great Stuart painter of the time, "Paint me as I am. If you leave out the scars and wrinkles I will not pay you a shilling." "Paint me, wart and all." If anyone had suggested that in order to increase his beauty the wart and other blemishes should foe removed by taking off his head, I can well imagine the sentiments he would have expressed. But the .hill, and the resolution which has been dropped, both proposed to sacrifice the .principle for the sake of the administration of that principle.

speechtext:
I will answer my hon. friend's question; I will not shirk it in the least. I have given one answer to the first proposition, that the Civil Service Act was a relic of war hysteria. Another answer, given by my friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland), seems most conclusive and convincing. He showed that the principle of the act was laid down in 1907, seven years before the war broke out, by Sir Robert Borden in the Halifax platform, and

was re-affirmed by Sir George Foster in 1903 before the first rumblings of the 1914 war were heard. Even if you put the first signs of the great war at the annexation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as some of us did at the time, the answer still applies. Seven years before the war this principle was proclaimed, and it was reasserted one year later.
I was not in Canada in 1907; I only came in 1912. But I remember that when I took an interest in provincial and federal politics in the beginning of 1913, almost as soon as I arrived in the city where I still live, I discovered that there were two problems which obsessed the minds of the Conservatives of Alberta. One of them was the return of their natural resources, for which *they were fighting, and the other was the introduction of a proper civil service system that would do away with the abominable system of patronage. I flung myself heart and soul into the fray in support of the second of these proposals, and in 1913 I had an opportunity to assert to a large assembly in Edmonton that the .people of Canada might as well expect to get decent public service from their civil servants under the patronage system as they might expect to distil attar of roses from a skunk. Perhaps that is a figure of speech more forcible than refined, but it is absolutely true. I am not reflecting upon the civil servants of 1912 or 1913, or any other year up to 1918.

Will the hon. gentleman
permit a question? I think he compared the civil service -of to-day with attar of roses.

I did not compare the civil
