At any rate this is the
question I wish to ask: Does the hon. gentleman consider that the personnel of the outside service to-day is more efficient than it was twenty years ago?

subtopic: EXCLUSION OF OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OF ACT.
speechtext:
I am not saying they are more efficient; I am saying that I do not reflect upon the civil service of 1912 or 1913 or subsequent years to 1918. In many respects we were given good service, but we did not get it because of the principle of patronage. We got it in spite of that principle, and because of the fact that notwithstanding the patronage, ordinary men are honest, and ordinary men want to perform the duties for which they are paid, however abominable the system under which they are appointed and maintained in office.
There was a second proposition made by my hon. friend from Muskoka-Ontario,

Civil Service Act-Mr. Bury
which brings me to the answering of the question he put to me a few minutes ago. He made the statement that the reason why we should change the present system and go back to patronage in respect to the outside service was that the member for the constituency was best fitted to say who should fill positions in that constituency. That was a staggering proposition to me. Perhaps I have not been in the house long enough to sustain shocks of that kind, but when he made that statement I indulged in a little introspection. I began to argue, "Well, if the member of a constituency is the man most capable of saying who should fill positions in the outside service, or in any part of the service, it would appear to follow that if a member is not the man most capable of saying who should fill positions, he should not be the member; he is out of his place." I began to wonder whether after all I was properly in my place in this house because I could not convince myself honestly that I was most capable of filling all civil service positions in the city of Edmonton. Now you know it is rather a serious thing to undermine the confidence of a member of parliament in his divine right to sit in the House of Commons. We are all so perfectly certain that our election made us the proper representatives of our constituencies, that we are the best fitted to represent the people there, and it is not nice to have that confidence undermined. But the doubt did not trouble me very long because I have come to the conclusion that it is no part of the business of any member of the House of Commons to make appointments to the civil service. It is no part of representative government; it has no connection with the principle of representative government. That is the answer I make to my hon. friend's question which he put to me a few minutes ago. It is no part of the principle of representative government, no part of the democratic principle that the members of the House of Commons should appoint the civil servants of the country. If that proposition were true, then the ideal towards which we should strive, in the form of our civil service, we should get from the United States instead of from the mother country; and if I had to choose the line of direction along which I should wish the civil service of Canada to develop, it would certainly not be southward but towards the other side of the Atlantic, towards the motherland which has built up a civil service second to none in the world. England has been working on the civil service problem since 1855. She has had commission after commission since that time. I have the list of them here but I will not detain the house by reading it.
Let me say, however, that there is no people that has the genius for practical government in so great a degree as the British people, and there is no phase of public life in which the people of Great Britain show their practical sense so well as in the sphere of administration. And they have shown it in its full essence and flower in their civil service system. That is one reason why I should prefer, instead of the amendment moved by the Minister of Justice and the appointment of a committee of the house to inquire into this subject, that a commissioner be sent over to study the English system of civil service on the spot, to meet the civil servants of England on the spot, and on the spot to see how that system works. He could then report to the government what he had discovered in regard to the methods of operation of that system.
Let me quote the words of Sir William Clark, High Commissioner for Great Britain in Canada, in an address given at a luncheon on May 29 to the Civil Service Federation. He said:
Someone will always grumble whatever the system may be, but I have no hesitation in saying that ours commands the general confidence of the service

That is a most important thing; but can you honestly say that the present system in Canada has secured and holds the confidence of the majority of the civil servants of Canada? I cannot say so from my little experience and from the expressions of sentiment that have come to me from one and another of them.
-and as civil servants you will agree that confidence in this respect is wholly essential for the maintenance of service morale.
But if the argument is true that the member of the constituency is the best man to make appointments, the man most capable of making them, I am faced with grave difficulties. In my constituency there is a post office and I venture to say that, if I started to make appointments to that post office, the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) would come and say to me, "Bury, this is not the post office of East Edmonton but the post office of the city of Edmonton, and I should have a say, just as much as you, in the appointments that are made in the city of Edmonton". There are Indian reserves that may lie on the border of a constituency. It may be that an Indian reserve spreads into another constituency. Well, who is to determine the appointee there ? Let me ask the house another question. If that principle is true, why stop at the outside civil service? Why leave poor Ottawa out? If the member

Civil Service Act-Mr. Bury

is the best man to make appointments in the outside civil service, why not in the inside as well? I cannot see why there should be a distinction. I cannot justify the discrimination against the city of Ottawa and the large number of civil servants who make up the civil service staff in this city.
The ideal of a civil service is twofold: to get the best men and to get from the best men the best service which each of them can give. And I venture to say that we will attain neither end through a system of patronage. You will not get the best men.. Often the best men in a- constituency have no particular regard for politics at all; they are not interested in politics. They occupy towards politics the same relation that the great mass of the people do who are not partisans on either side, the people who swing elections. I have tried again and again to get my people to understand that elections are not won or lost by the partisans but are won or lost by the movement of the great non-partisan body of the electors of the country who must be convinced of the soundness and the justice of a policy before they will support it. The best men in any constituency may not be partisans. They may say to the partisans of a political organization, as Mercutio said:
A plague o' both your houses . . .
They have made worms' meat of me.
A plague o' both your houses-they have made politicians' meat of me; between the two of you I am killed. That is or may be the attitude of the best man in the constituency, and if that is true what chance has he of appointment? We are not living in the millenium; we are not Hiving under conditions of Utopia; and while I am willing to admit that I have not noticed any barbed tails or cloven hoofs, I have not heard the rustle of any wings on either side of the house. I know perfectly well what would happen. Whatever hon. members may say, and however much they may protest that the principle of patronage would be honestly and honourably exercised, human nature being human nature and political exigencies being political exigencies, in the heat of on election or in the orisis of one approaching, I know perfectly well what would happen, and from the crown of my head to the sole of my feet I am opposed to any movement looking to the return of the patronage system. You will not get the best men. What kind of service are you going to get? The essential for good services is singleness of eye. Will you get it? No; every one in the service will have one eye on the results of the next election and the other on his work; one eye will be on his duties and the

other on the movement of political sentiment throughout his particular constituency and throughout the country. Instead of singleness of eye we shall develop what might be termed the civil service squint; and may we be forever preserved from that. There can be singleness of eye only when a man knows that as long as he is doing his duty well and faithfully, no power, political or otherwise, can disturb him. We will never have the best service available until that is a fact.
It is said that it is not proposed to give a member the power to dismiss. Why not? If he is the best man to appoint, why is he not the best man to dismiss? Where are we going to draw the line, and what right have we to draw a line? Is a man who has won a federal riding by one, two, three or a half dozen votes to be divinely invested with some strange power which he did not have before the election to enable him to know who is the best man to appoint? If so, then I ask: why is he not the proper person to dismiss? Once the power of appointment is given it will not be very long before the power of dismissal creeps in. Even if it did not, it would be hanging over the heads of the civil servants. There would be continual temptation to curry favour because they would feel they were at the mercy of political tides and political sentiments; they would feel they were at the mercy of some man who through some passing wave in the tide of political feeling had been put into power.
I intend to support the amendment of the hon. Minister of Justice, not because I believe it to be the beet amendment possible, but because I hope that when its purpose is effectuated a commission will be sent to England to obtain first hand information in connection with the working of the English civil service.
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Bury) has given to the house his reasons for supporting the amendment of the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), I should supply to the house some evidence to show the disregard into which the Civil Service Act has fallen. The evidence which I will present does not cover all members of the cabinet, as it would take such a long time to make a complete investigation, but may I give a few instances in connection with the department of the Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) which, I think, will dumbfound hon. members on both sides of the house.
On November 23, 1930, the minister stated that fanaticism was Canada's worst enemy,

Civil Service Act-Mr. Pouliot
and in the same month he declared that he would defend a faithful employee of the government against even his own personal friends. That is, if a Conservative member or a Conservative defeated candidate asked for the dismissal of an honest employee, the Postmaster General would reply: Shut up, do not say a word; that man is a faithful employee and I am bound to defend him against your complaint; you have no reason to complain and I will stand by my promise. When in Cornwall the minister made a very nice speech and he told of how his heart bled when anyone mentioned dismissals. He said he had the courage not to dismiss a faithful employee who was doing his duty. I should like to quote from a translation of that speech, as follows:
From the moment I took office as Postmaster General, I promised justice, economy and honest administration. On that occasion I declared that the civil servant, postmaster or other employee who performed his duties as required and who had not violated the law by taking an active part in politics had nothing to fear from me, that I would protect him even against my own friends. The postmaster who did not take part in perpetrating an injustice by accepting the place of one of his fellow citizens, unjustly dismissed, had nothing to fear. The letter carrier who in the fulfilment of his duties of distributing mail from door to door did not become the active agent of any political party, had nothing to fear.
In presenting this evidence to the house I will not mention names as I have no desire to reflect on anyone, but any hon. member who desires particular information can obtain it.
In a certain country post office the postmaster had a daughter of about sixteen or seventeen years of age. This daughter frequently visited the post office and she became very much interested in the correspondence of the boys and girls of the village. One day a friend borrowed her coat and found it to be extra heavy on one side. Upon investigation she found in one of the pockets between fifty or sixty letters addressed to different boys and girls in the neighbourhood. Complaints were made, the postmaster was dismissed and another appointment made by the Civil Service Commission. Was this man unjustly dismissed? His daughter had intercepted letters in the post office, and what happened to him was not because of his politics. He lost his job. He was replaced by a competent man. Last year there was an investigation about the latter. Ten witnesses were heard. One of them was this man's predecessor, the former postmaster, who had lost the post office. What was his evidence? He said: I have no knowledge that 41761-351
the postmaster is guilty of political partisanship. And that man lives the second door away from the post office. He had no reason at all for not telling the commissioner what he knew about the postmaster who had succeeded him, because he knew that he had lost the postmastership on account of the doings of his daughter. He was under oath before the commissioner and he told the truth, and that was his evidence. The mayor of the municipality, who is a Conservative chieftain or leader, gave exactly the same evidence. Nine witnesses out of ten gave exactly the same evidence. Only one witness stated that the postmaster had shown around a paper giving figures as to what the local member had obtained for his constituency, and that was denied right off by another witness. The commissioner asked the witness: Did the postmaster canvass you to vote for the candidate? The witness said no, and the commissioner came back and said: Are you sure that he did not canvass you? The witness again said no. The commissioner then asked: Do you remember that he did not canvass you? And the witness said no,
I do not remember that. Here is his statement as drafted by the commissioner:
I do not recall having talked politics with the postmaster at the post office. I am his brother-in-law.
The only witness who gave that so-called evidence against the postmaster was a newcomer to the village. He came from another parish where he had left no good souvenirs. He was the only one who made a complaint against the postmaster and he was interested in making it. His evidence was not corroborated, on the contrary was denied. What happened? The postmaster, who is a former mayor of the municipality, was dismissed, and he was replaced by the very same man who had accused him, the only one who had accused him, in spite of the fact that all the Conservative leaders in the community who lived near to him said that to their knowledge he had taken no part in politics.
The Postmaster General says:
The postmaster who did not take part in perpetrating an injustice by accepting the place of one of his fellow citizens, unjustly dismissed, had nothing to fear. The civil servant, postmaster or other employee who performed his duties as required and who had not violated the law by taking an active part in politics had nothing to fear from me, that I would protect him even against my own friends.
In this case the majority of the favourable witnesses were the friends, and the best friends, of the Postmaster General. They were against dismissal, but evidently the

Civil Service Act-Mr. Pouliot
Postmaster General acted against his own friends in that case. A petition was signed by a large majority of the people within the post office area, by the cure and many others to prevent a change of post office, but it was disregarded and the postmastership was given to a man who had made an interested and a false complaint against the postmaster. What I have said so far is only to make the mouths water of those hon. gentlemen who are honouring me with their attention. Now I have something much nicer to tell them.
As every member of this house knows, the Post Office Department has sent to all postmasters throughout the country a circular letter advising them that they are strictly forbidden to take any part in federal or provincial elections, and that those who had done so had better resign in order to save the cost of an expensive investigation.
Here is the case of a postmaster at a place I will name, St. Eusebe-de-Cabano. The postmaster, who was also mayor, received such a circular letter and he resigned. What happened? He was replaced by a man whom I will name, and for a very good reason, as the hon. members will see. He is called Paul Langlois, and he replaced the former postmaster on June 30, 1931. A month and a half later or so the provincial elections were taking place in the province of Quebec, and Mr. Langlois could not show in any better way his gratitude to the Postmaster General than by canvassing for the provincial Conservative party. Langlois was replacing a man who had received a notice of dismissal because he was supposed to have taken some part in the election, whether federal or provincial I do not know. Here is what he did, and I am very sorry that the hon. Postmaster General has left the house with his portfolio under his arm. I hope that some of his friends will call him back here so that he can hear what I am saying.
On or about August 12 of last year Langlois, the postmaster, went to Riviere-Bleue in his car to get some liquor to be used in canvassing. He was accompanied by three men named Thimothee Dube, Pierre Dube and Jos. Albert Dube. I do not wonder what their political affiliations are, but naturally at election time one is rather suspicious about such joy rides. When they came back with the liquor, Dube's rig was at Langlois', and the new postmaster transferred the liquor from the auto to the rig, probably keeping some for his own use. Though all this took place at night, it was clearly witnessed by someone who reported it very accurately. I would ask the Postmaster General this ques-
(Mr. Pouliot.]
tion:	If a man must resign his position as
postmaster upon a charge not specified but perhaps because he has been accused of canvassing in the federal or provincial elections, will the Postmaster General take' the same steps with regard to a postmaster who has carried liquor in his own car to be used in political canvassing?
If the mouths of my hon. friends opposite water a little bit, I have something even more relishing ito tell them. In my constituency there is a parish named Sully, situated on the Transcontinental railway. There were rumours abroad that the postmaster of that place was to be dismissed). He also was mayor, and a very dignified gentleman who did not incur any blame, so far as I know. His removal seems to have been founded on the old principle that to the victor belongs the spoils, and although the Conservative candidate was defeated he was, nevertheless, the victor so far as the granting of postal offices to this or that one was concerned.
In that parish there was another gentleman named Isidore Jean, a returned soldier whose regimental number was 2245410. He served two years at the front, performed his duty as a good soldier, and as the parish is not very large he knew there were some intrigues afoot to dismiss the postmaster. Naturally, as charity begins at home he thought he had better take his chance and, as a result, wrote to the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. MacLaren), to the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and to the Postmaster General, saying, in effect, "If you intend to dismiss the postmaster in charge of the post office I shall be very happy to file my application for that position." Although the letter is in the French language, as it is not very long I shall read it. This letter is from Isidore Jean to the Postmaster General, and is dated November 2, 1931:
(Translation):
Honorable sir,
On February 17, 1931, the right hon. Prime Minister's secretary wrote to me that he had forwarded to you my application for the post of postmaster at Sully in the event of this position becoming vacant.
On October 5, the same gentleman suggested that 1 should communicate directly with the secretary of the Civil Service Commission and with yourself, since you have complete jurisdiction over your department.
On October 28, the Minister of Pensions' secretary wrote to me that he had forwarded to you my letter and the others attached for your kind consideration.
On March 4, 1931, your acting deputy minister wrote to me that there was no vacancy in the post office at Sully at that time and that should it become necessary to make a

Civil Service Act-Mr. Pouliot
change the appointment of the new incumbent would be made by the Civil Service Commission. He further added that my application had been noted and that it would be referred to the commission should the circumstances warrant it.
On September 28, your deputy minister wrote to me that should it be necessary to make a change at Sully, the permanent appointment of the future incumbent would be made by the Civil Service Commission which would advertise publicly the vacancy occurring in that locality, and that the minister had taken careful note of my application.
On October 14, your deputy minister again wrote to me that my application had been referred to him by the private secretary of the minister and that he wished to draw my attention to his letter of September 28.
The officials of your department wrote to me on three different occasions this year that in the event of a vacancy occurring the appointment of a postmaster at Sully would be made by the Civil Service Commission. Should you decide to make a temporary appointment, while awaiting the ratification of this appointment by the Civil Service Commission, may I have the honour to remind you of my application for the post of temporary postmaster at Sully, in case you decided to replace the present postmaster, and this, on the score of my record of services at the front where I fought during two years. My regimental number is the following: 2245410.
I am, sir,
Your grateful servant
(Sgd.) Isidore Jean.
What happened? That man was told by the departments of Pensions and National Health and of the Postmaster General that in the event of a dismissal, and a vacancy in the post office referred to, the matter would come before the Civil Service Commission for the nomination of a new postmaster. What was done? The application of the man who had a creditable war record was entirely disregarded, and the Postmaster General appointed another man who had had no service at the front. In my view this would have been a fit case to bring before the British Empire Service League to show that the Postmaster General paid no attention to the soldier's application to fill the vacancy which occurred in that post office. This particular case deserved serious consideration because the applicant was a poor soldier who is at present unemployed; therefore the reasons for his appointment were two-fold. It is indeed unfortunate that his application was disregarded by the Postmaster General in spite of and against the provisions of the Civil Service Act.
Not only did the protege of the Postmaster General carry liquor in times of provincial elections, and not only does he disregard the Civil Service Act so far as it applies to veterans, but there is something to relate even better than that. It is this: My contention is that in this country public offices should be held either by Canadians by birth or Canadians by naturalization, and that aliens should not be allowed to occupy public offices. I have in mind an instance which occurred at Pointe Lebel, and because that place is in the constituency of Charlevoix-Saguenay I am sure my hon. friend from that constituency (Mr. Casgrain) will be pleased to hear about it. The former postmaster was dismissed and replaced by a man named Grenier. That man came from France some years ago, and I am told from reliable sources that he has never been naturalized. I communicated with the Department of the Secretary of State to learn if Grenier of Pointe Lebel was naturalized. I am under the impression that my hon. friend from Charlevoix-Saguenay will vouch for my statement that this man Grenier came from France some years ago, and was never naturalized. When we came to the naturalization branch of the Department of the Secretary of State we asked if they had any record of Grenier, and they replied that from the year 1915, when records were first kept they had no record. I was told to communicate with the Bureau of Statistics, but when I approached that branch of the service I was answered that information could not be given because the information on the sheets filled out for statistical purposes, or for. purposes of census, was given in strict confidence. As a result I could not get the information I desired. The evidence, so far, is that there is no record of Grenier in the Department of the Secretary of State and it is a fact that Grenier is not a Canadian by birth or naturalization and is not entitled to public office. Rather than allow Canadians by birth or naturalization to enjoy public offices the Postmaster General deprives them of their rights and gives preference to foreigners. It is not at all surprising that the returned soldier feels he is not receiving fair treatment.
But there is more than that Mr. Speaker. Last year, speaking on the budget, my hon. friend, then Minister of Fisheries, now Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), said:
I am sure my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) and his leader would have been the first to take exception with, during the last session under the previous government, hon. members on the other side of the house who had fastened the responsibility upon the then government for the utterances of my hon- friend from Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), when he made attacks upon the premier of the province of Quebec.
Was he referring to a memorandum based on the fact that aliens in the province of Quebec were entitled by statute to be ap-

Civil Service Act-Mr. Brown
pointed to public office? I communicated with the premiers of 'the other eight provinces asking what stand they took in the matter, and this is the answer I received from the hon. gentleman who was then premier of Nova Scotia and is now Minister of Finance in this government:
Absence from my office in other portions of the province has prevented me from making earlier acknowledgment of your letter of June 26th.
The ground you take with respect to the holding of office by aliens is, in my opinion, undoubtedly sound.
I hope my hon. friend will have the courage to stand by the views he then expressed and support me in my demand that the Postmaster General be required to furnish all available information about that man Grenier, as to whether he lives under a false name, when he came to this country, when he was naturalized. and on whose recommendation he received his appointment.
Let me conclude my remarks in the sweet language of France by giving an excerpt from an article published by the hon. Postmaster General:
Je le repete, avouons franehement nos erreurs afin de benefieier autant que possible meme de nos fautes.
This may be translated:
Let us be frank about our mistakes in order that we may get as much benefit as possible from them.
A fine sentiment! I hope he will have those words recorded in homespun and place them in front of his desk that he may ponder them frequently. I must ask the Postmaster General to be serious. Most of his colleagues seem to have greater respect for the Civil Service Act. So should he. He is not a bad man. He should be strong enough to resist his friends. I am sure that when he made the promise he was confident of his strength to keep it as a man. Now, why doesn't he do so? He should do it for the reason expressed by 'the hon. member for East Edmonton. I listened with very much interest to the hon. member's speech. He said it would be a very bad thing for the civil service if civil servants could not live in peace and be free of anxiety about their future, that only in this way could they give the thorough service that the country expected from them. I submit that that is a very strong argument in favour of the Postmaster General doing what he is requested to do. The reason is that after a man has been in the cavil service for a number of years it is difficult for him to return to his former occupation. What I am

trying to convey is well-expressed in French -those men become "deracines." The civil service of Canada is as good as that of any other country in the world, and it should be protected against those greedy and lazy persons who by intrigue seek to bring about the dismissal of industrious and capable civil servants in order that they may be appointed to the vacancies so created. I hope tomorrow morning, Mr. Speaker, the Postmaster General, who is not in his seat to-night, will read Hansard and take heed of what has been said this evening.

Mr. Speaker, had the motion for second reading of the bill been proceeded with I should have been compelled to vote against it. I wish to express the pleasure I derived from the speech delivered by the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Bury). I am sure we all regret that the occasions are not more numerous when he participates in debate. Those of us who were here with him in the hectic session of 1926 will remember the many fine speeches he then delivered, and I feel certain we regret that the limitations imposed upon a supporter of the government prevent us from hearing the hon. gentleman oftener.
I am heartily in sympathy with the sentiments he expressed. I should like also to commend the speech made by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland), in which he set before us very clearly the position with regard to the Civil Service Commission. I believe I am safe in making the statement that only a minority on either side of the house is in favour of doing away with the Civil Service Act and returning to the old patronage system. I know that is true of this side of the house, and I am happy to believe from the speeches made to-night that it is also true of the other side. I have always been strongly opposed to the patronage system. While it may be true that the act is not working perfectly at present, there is no reason to suppose that as time goes on it may not be administered more efficiently. I think there is every reason why an investigation into the working of the act should be undertaken. Undoubtedly there are just causes for complaint, and if these were threshed out before a committee I hope the result would be beneficial to the service as a whole.
I do not think the government has handled this matter in the best possible way. At the outset they very well could have removed from the minds of hon. members any fear of the possibility of the merit system being destroyed. Perhaps it was necessary to

Civil Service Act-Mr. McGibbon
give the hon. member for Dorchester an opportunity to fulfil the pledge which undoubtedly he made to his constituents, that he would do his best to secure a return to the patronage system. I think we had his own word for it last session that he made such a pledge, and perhaps it was necessary that he should be allowed an opportunity to keep it. At the same time I think if a little different course had been pursued by the government we would have had our minds satisfied on this question at an earlier time, and perhaps there would not have been the necessity for so much discussion on the merits of the case.

subtopic: EXCLUSION OF OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OF ACT.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to take any part in this debate until a number of hon. members seemed to prefer to discuss me rather than the question before the house. One of the principal objections has been that the member is not the man best qualified to make any appointment that may be necessary in his riding. The hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Bury) was particularly strong on this point. I am quite willing to concede, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member is capable of speaking for himself, and I have no quarrel with the decision he makes when he says he is not capable of making the appointments that may be necessary in his constituency. That is his prerogative and his privilege; as he sits in judgment upon his own capabilities and renders a verdict of that nature, far be it from me to dispute its accuracy. I think possibly that is quite true, but the unfortunate thing is that in such a case he is not the one who suffers; the people who send him here suffer, and that is rather too bad. It is too bad that any riding in Canada should have a representative who admits on the floor of the house that he is incapable of filling positions which may become vacant in that riding.

I did not say I was incapable
of doing so; I said I was not the person best fitted to make the appointments.

subtopic: EXCLUSION OF OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OF ACT.
speechtext: My hon. friend says he is not the best person, so obviously he is not the best member.

subtopic: EXCLUSION OF OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OF ACT.
speechtext: He was thinking of you [DOT]as the best.

speechtext: I have no objection to my hon. friend speaking for himself, but I do object to him speaking for me. He is not capable of doing that. I say further, Mr. Speaker, that this is not a matter of appointments or of patronage; there is a bigger question involved It is a question of the principle of responsible government.

subtopic: EXCLUSION OF OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OF ACT.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: EXCLUSION OF OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OF ACT.
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power); I have always admired his judgment and found it good. I take that very seriously. Responsible government is something for which great struggles have been waged in the past in every country in the world. The three great objects of the revolution of 1690 were responsible government, the supremacy of the House of Commons and the assurance that the House of Commons should represent the voice of the people.
In connection with these appointments, who is responsible? Is there any responsibility any place?

subtopic: EXCLUSION OF OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OF ACT.
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?

subtopic: EXCLUSION OF OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OF ACT.
speechtext: Do not make it too hard.

subtopic: EXCLUSION OF OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OF ACT.
speechtext: Is there not responsible government in Great Britain?

subtopic: EXCLUSION OF OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OF ACT.
speechtext:
Yes, but Great Britain has not a civil service like ours. The hon. member started to discuss the civil service of Great Britain; he only showed that he did not know anything about it. I object to these men speaking for me; I object to them speaking for the people in my riding, and in spite of what the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) has said I believe that three-quarters of the members of this house would vote for this motion if they were given a free ballot. It is only party exigencies that keep them from doing so. They know it is the best thing.
Look at the appointments which 'have been made by this Civil Service Commission. Does anyone in the house not remember what happened in the last few years, when the Postmaster General rose in his place and told of the hundreds of postmasters who had been dismissed because of shortages in their funds? Does that reflect great credit upon the Civil Service Commission? Within the last week or so we have had a second scandal aired. Did we have that sort of thing in the past? Would not appointments made in the past by representatives of the people compare favourably with those that have been made by the Civil Service Commission?
Another objection I have is this: I do not like the communications which the civil service of Ottawa have had the impudence to mail to me and other members of the

Civil Service Act-Mr. McGibbon
House of Commons. I am not seeking to interfere with tlhe inside service, and I say they have no business to interfere with the service in my riding. If there is one thing that disgusts me more than another it is the attitude that has been shown by the civil service of Ottawa towards the proposed cut in their salaries. Where is the man or woman in this country to-day making as much as they were making three or four years ago? Let me say further that more than 99 per cent of the money which pays these civil servants comes from people outside of this city. The civil service does not belong entirely to the city of Ottawa; it belongs to the Dominion of Canada. They should remember that it gives them work in good times and bad, in good weather and 'bad. They are not like the people we are feeding a,t the public expense in northern Ontario to-day, who find their pay docked for every sitormy day when they cannot work. I say, sir, I have been disgusted with their attitude in a crisis of this kind when this country, like every other country in the world, is in financial difficulties. They are not willing to take voluntarily and joyfully a out that is not equal to the decrease in the cost of living.

subtopic: EXCLUSION OF OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OF ACT.
speechtext:
Has my hon. friend
read the speech from the throne which states that the country is very prosperous?

subtopic: EXCLUSION OF OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OF ACT.
speechtext:
I fail to see any intelligent connection between that question and the remarks I was making.
I want to say again, sir, that this is not a matter of patronage. I do not think there is any hon. member of this house who wants the disagreeable job of making appointments. As I have said, patronage will kill any member if he gets enough of it; there is no doubt about that. But the people in my riding want me to assume that responsibility and I should be a coward if I were not prepared to do so. They want me to be their representative and they want me because .they have some control over me; and when the day comes that I do not do what they want they will put me out. But they have no control, nor has any other constituency any control over the people who are making appointments to-day. And, Mr. Speaker, patronage has not been done away with. Why do we try to fool ourselves? Every hon. member knows that it has not been done away with. Every hon. member knows also that the educational test or the merit test in the outside service is not worth a snap of the finger.
I agree with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) in that speech he made a year ago, that, too much has been taken

away from the people's representatives. I believe that, with profit to this country, some of that responsibility could be restored. Everyone knows that when a member has to make an appointment he is going to make the best he can. I shall be told that when the Conservatives are in power a Conservative will be appointed. I grant you that; he would be in my riding anyway. But supposing there were a better one in the Liberal party-

subtopic: EXCLUSION OF OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OF ACT.
speechtext: You would not appoint him.

subtopic: EXCLUSION OF OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OF ACT.
speechtext:
Never mind whether I would appoint him or not. But I contend that if you got the second best man in every riding in this country you would get a higher class than under the Civil Service Commission. I am sometimes disgusted at the way debates will turn and twist un this house. It seems that at times one leader will throw it this way and another will give it a twist in some other direction ; and then we get on a high moral plane as in this debate and almost immortalize the Civil Service Commission, though it has been one of the disgraceful black spots on the government of the country. Everyone knows it. Where could you find anything such as was exhibited in the courts a little while ago?
I do not want the house or the country to think that I want the job of going out and beheading .people. Decent people-and members of parliament are decent-do not do that sort of thing. Moreover, when a man is in a position for three or four years he loses connection with the past, and no decent member of parliament is going to kick him out even if he belongs to the other party. I have been disgusted with that argument. I do not believe there is a man in this house who would do such a thing without grave cause, and then he would do it very reluctantly. For these reasons I am glad that this question is going to a committee where all phases of it can be discussed, and when the committee reports to the house no doubt it will be able to advise along better lines.

And, in that case, would he believe in the system which has been followed at times, of the defeated candidate on the government side

receiving that power of making these appointments although the people had rejected him as

speechtext: That is not hard to answer. I have said three or four times that personally I do not care where the member sits. But there is this to be said about it. Mr. Speaker, the opportunity of supporting the bill of my bon. friend and neighbour the member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) would have pieiased me much, unfortunately, I fear this opportunity will not be afforded to us, as the amendment moved by the hon. Minister of Justice is probably tantamount to full burial honours for the bill.
I would have been pleased, I stated, to be given the opportunity of supporting the bill because, two years hence, it would have given us a chance of rectifying the injustice perpetrated by this government which dismissed, without reasons and contrary to the Civil Service Act, a considerable number of employees.
I entirely agree with the sponsor of this bill and with my hon. friend the member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis) in their statement that the Civil Service Act rests on a false principle. I listened attentively to my bon. friend from Dorchester when he introduced his bill. He established rather a strong 'Case against the Civil Service Act and the commission. I expected to hear him ask for the repeal of the act and the disestablishment of the Civil Service Commission. I was amazed in reading over his bill to find that he did not recommend the repeal of the act, not even the suppression of the commission, but simply requested the exclusion of the outside service from the operation of the act. However, I would have supported this measure because it is a step forward in the -right direction.
Again do I state, the Civil Service Act rests on a false principle. If the government is vested with the responsibilities of the administration, the public employees share with the government in this administration of the affairs of the country. If the government is to be held responsible for the work of its co-operators, I fail to understand why it would not be so as regards their appointment and their selection as they think proper. Moreover this act lends itself to deceit as the hon. member for
St. Denis (Mr. Denis) stated' just now; it is one of these insincere measures that governments enact once in a while with the fixed mental reservation of disregarding it. The election act is another instance; the government themselves are the main offenders. They, themselves, have made the most frequent inroads on the provisions of the Civil Service Act, they are the first to disregard it and to show their contempt.
To illustrate my argument, let me cite two cases. First, I shall draw the attention of members to the Votes and Proceedings of this house, of July 30, 1931, at page 661:
Weights and measures inspection (including International Bureau of Weights and Measures)

further amount required for the salary, including the appointment of Charles Hippolyte Couture, Inspector of Weights and Measures, Quebec district, Quebec city, at $1,560 per annum, from April 1, 1931, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Civil Service Act.
The following are the facts: If I am well informed, there was a vacancy in the Bureau of Weights and Measures, at Quebec. The Civil Sendee Commission, having advertised the position, and received applications, held an examination, after which a list of those eligible was drawn. At the head of this list was a veteran by the name of Mathieu Parrot, of Quebec city. Parrot was awarded 86 points, he was at the head of this list, moreover, he was given the preference owing to his being a veteran. This did not suit Couture's backer who wanted to have him appointed, at all costs. It was then that his supporter found a flaw in the Civil Service Act, as I have just pointed out, and had his friend appointed, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Civil Service Act, and against the wishes of the commission itself. This is a case where the government themselves disregarded the Civil Service Act.
On the same day by a special vote, another appointment was made contrary to the Act; this is another instance of the disregard of the legislation enacted by the government. You will find in the Votes and Proceedings of the same date, page 656, the following:
To appoint hereby J. L. A. Tanguay, a clerk, grade i, in the minister's office at Quebec from August 7, 1930, at $1,860 per annum, $3,100.
I must mention, by the way, that our friends who so highly criticized a certain act of the Quebec legislature because it had a retroactive effect, were in no way bashful in the present case to give a retroactive effect to this appointment. This is a further instance showing how the government conforms to the laws they enact. We therefore have a right to say that

Civil Service Act-Mr. Boulanger
the Civil Service Act is utterly hypocritical, and that the government is the first to disregard its provisions. Let me further add that these two gentlemen appointed by a special vote of the house, one on the motion of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), the other on the motion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), are two common election workers (cabaleurs) of the lowest order. They are, to all intents, political appointments. Couture, again, if I am well informed, was dismissed in 1926, because he was the cause of disorder at a meeting held by the Hon. Lucien Cannon, in the county of Dorchester. He was employed, previous to that, by the weights and measures branch and lost his position for having taken an active part in politics and being the cause of disorder at a public meeting. One had recourse to this dodge or underhand dealing, after his dismissal for political partisanship, in order to reappoint him in the weights and measures branch, notwithstanding the Civil Service Commission's protest and in violation of the act, thereby doing a grave injustice to the veteran Mathieu Parrot.
Let us now examine the case of Tanguay with whom I am better acquainted, since he is a political organizer in my county. Tanguay was appointed to the minister's office as a fourth grade clerk. If I am well informed, Tanguay controls the patronage in Quebec, that is he is a middleman and performs the dirty work of the Conservative party. In my county a dozen postmasters were dismissed without cause, and contrary to the Civil Service Act, and, according to what I heard, these dismissals took place mainly at the request of Mr. Tanguay himself. At the last provincial election, in 1931, Mr. Tanguay was the principal speaker of the Conservative candidate in Bellechasse; he meddled in the election, spoke at all meetings and thereby took an active political part. I took upon myself the responsibility of denouncing him to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Bennett) , who through his secretary, wrote to me that he had referred my complaint to the Minister of Justice. The other day I inquired whether my complaint had been received, whether an inquiry would be held and Tanguay dismissed, in the event of my complaint being substantiated. The Minister of Justice informed me that the Department of Justice had no information with respect to the complaint lodged against Tanguay. Nevertheless, it had been lodged with the Prime Minister, and his secretary had written to me that it had been referred to the Minister of Justice. Let us suppose, for a moment, 
that the Minister of Justice had not received this complaint, the question which I placed on the orders of the day, some time ago, was a sufficient notice to the government of my complaint of political partisanship lodged against Tanguay, and the government is bound, in honour, equity and justice, after occasionally dismissing public employees for trivial causes, to hold an inquiry on a complaint lodged by a member of parliament and supported by the evidence.
The government should order an inquiry and dismiss this employee, if my complaint is well grounded.
The postmaster of Beaumont was dismissed under the plea thait he had decorated his residence on polling day, in September 1926, but, on that day the person referred to was not yet appointed as postmaster; he was only appointed the following month.
The postmaster at LaDurantaye was dismissed, because his son, who is married and is not living with his father had in his automobile-the automobile of the son, not that of the father-the photograph of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). An inquiry was held by three defeated candidates. You may judge how slim were the chances of this poor postmaster in such an inquiry 1 A large number of postmasters were dismissed without cause, and here is a public employee in receipt of $1,860 per year, who openly and brazenly takes part in a political campaign. A complaint is lodged against him by a member of parliament, a complaint founded in fact, and it is impossible to obtain an inquiry; we cannot even obtain a straight and honest answer from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) to a question put to him the other day with reference to this matter.
I protest, sir. against such government methods, especially when to all purposes it approves the Civil Service Act. Since the government is opposed to the repeal of this act, why should it not be the first to comply with the letter and spirit of the act, and grant to civil servants, who are so unfortunate as to be Liberals, all the protection to which they are entitled.
The government should also see that civil servants whom they appoint conform to the law. Since it is wrong for a Liberal to be even suspected of political partisanship, surely civil servants appointed by the government should themselves bow to the law and not be guilty of obvious and glaring irregularities as those referred to.
Although opposed to the principle of the Civil Service Act, I am in favour of having a commission in order to classify candidates

Canadian National Railways-Finances
and have them undergo a test. I simply ask that appointments be subject to the jurisdiction of the government; that the latter be held responsible and given the final word m such matters.
It is held that the Civil Service Act was passed with a view of abolishing the patronage system, this is a mistake. Patronage has not been abolished, it has simply changed hands. It was taken away from members and placed in the hands of heads of departments, chief clerks and high officials. The civil service commission should be given a competent board of examiners and inspectors, it should control the tests of candidates to the various positions and it should be given the necessary authority to rate these candidates. At present, the commission has not the required staff to carry on this work. Examinations and classification are being looked after by civil servants. The latter themselves control the patronage. When an appointment is to be made, the commission sends all the examination papers to the chief clerk concerned and it is the latter himself who determines the grade and makes the appointment. Again do I state patronage has not been abolished, it has simply changed hands; it is replaced by a system of deceit as the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis) stated a short while ago-and productive of deception; it is therefore only reasonable that this system be changed.
Amendment (Mr. Guthrie) agreed to.
Motion (Mr. Gagnon) as amended agreed to.
